0.title: Give Us a King: The Book of 1 Samuel
0.overview:
First Samuel is one of the most dramatic, psychologically rich, and theologically profound books in the entire Bible. It spans roughly a century of Israel's history — from the birth of Samuel under the corrupt priesthood of Eli's sons, to the tragic deterioration of Saul and the breathtaking rise of David. At its center stands a single, epoch-making demand: Give us a king like all the nations (8:5). That cry is not merely a political request; it is a theological crisis, and God's response — they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them (8:7) — frames everything that follows.

The book is structured in three great movements. First, Samuel (chapters 1–7): the last judge, the transitional prophet-priest who holds a collapsing nation together by the sheer weight of his intercession and integrity. Second, Saul (chapters 8–15): the people's king, tall and impressive, chosen to satisfy human desire for outward glory, who cannot obey and cannot repent — a portrait of religion without heart. Third, David (chapters 16–31): the anointed one, the man after God's own heart, whose rise is as improbable as it is irresistible, tracked relentlessly by Saul's paranoid hatred and sustained only by covenant friendship and the Spirit of the Lord.

Christologically, 1 Samuel is a treasury. Hannah's prayer in chapter 2 is the seed of the Magnificat; her line — he will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed (2:10) — is the first use of mashiach in a clearly eschatological sense. Samuel embodies the triple office of prophet, priest, and judge that finds its perfect fulfillment in Jesus alone. The ark narratives (chs. 4–6) prophesy the glory departing and returning — Ichabod reversed by Emmanuel. And David: the shepherd-king, the anointed one upon whom the Spirit rushes, the champion who fights on behalf of his paralyzed people, the one who will not seize the kingdom by force — in every scene, the attentive reader sees the shape of One greater than David.

R. C. Sproul wrote that 1 Samuel shows us that God is not impressed by what impresses us. The book says it in seven words: Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (16:7). That inversion of human values — the youngest son anointed, the smooth stone over the giant's spear, the fugitive who becomes king — is the grammar of grace, and it will reach its apex when the carpenter's son from Nazareth is crowned on a cross.

1.title: The Barren Woman's Prayer
1.text: <sup>10</sup>She was deeply distressed and prayed to the LORD and wept bitterly. <sup>11</sup>And she vowed a vow and said, 'O LORD of hosts, if you will indeed look on the affliction of your servant and remember me and not forget your servant, but will give to your servant a son, then I will give him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor shall touch his head.' (ESV)
1.overview:
The book opens not in the throne room but in the heartbreak of a barren woman. Hannah's anguish is the hinge on which the entire history of the monarchy turns. God's method is always to work through weakness, through the impossible, through tears — and so the story of Israel's greatest prophet begins not with a royal decree but with a silent prayer in Shiloh's tabernacle. The literary structure is deliberate: Elkanah's divided household mirrors Israel's divided heart; Peninnah's provocation mirrors the nations' taunts; and Hannah's persistent, anguished faith models the prayer that God loves to answer. Alistair Begg notes that Hannah does not understand why God has closed her womb, but she knows to whom to bring her sorrow — and that knowledge is itself a great grace.

The chapter also introduces us to the priesthood in decay. Eli's sons are named in verse 3 — Hophni and Phinehas — a dark cloud on the horizon. Yet through this broken institution, God is quietly preparing the one who will replace it. The chapter ends with Hannah going home, eating, and her face no longer sad (v. 18) — she has prayed, been heard, and believed before the answer came. This is the theology of faith in miniature.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elkanah's household at Ramah: two wives, one favored and one barren, annual pilgrimage to Shiloh, and the silent grief that no earthly comfort can touch.
verseByVerse.theology: God sovereignly closes Hannah's womb (v. 5) — not as punishment but as preparation. The double portion Elkanah gives (v. 5) shows his love, yet love cannot solve what only God can open.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Barrenness carried social shame in Israel; a woman's worth was measured by children. Now: Many carry private griefs — infertility, longing, unanswered prayer — that no human comfort fully reaches.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a certain man of Ramathaim-zophim of the hill country of Ephraim whose name was Elkanah the son of Jeroham...
verseByVerse.commentary:
The opening genealogy anchors this story in real history. Ramathaim-zophim — later simply Ramah — is in the hill country of Ephraim, perhaps fifteen miles north of Jerusalem. The narrator traces Elkanah's lineage four generations back, establishing him as a man of standing and covenant connection. He is an Ephraimite by tribe, a Zuphite by clan — and his name, Elkanah, means 'God has created' or 'God has possessed.' Names in the Old Testament carry theological weight, and this one quietly announces the theme: all that Elkanah has — including the son about to be born — belongs to God.

Sinclair Ferguson observes that 1 Samuel opens at the ground level of ordinary family life, not at the heights of national politics. God's great redemptive purposes are being worked out in a household in the hill country. This is consistently the Bible's method: Abraham called from Ur, Moses hidden in a basket, the Word made flesh in a stable. The spectacular always grows from the ordinary when God is at work. The reader is invited to look at their own ordinary circumstances and ask: what is God growing here?

verseByVerse.quote: He had two wives. The name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other Peninnah. And Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children. Now this man used to go up year by year from his town to worship and to sacrifice to the LORD of hosts at Shiloh...
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two wives, one fruitful and one barren — the household is already divided. Polygamy in Scripture is never presented without its attendant sorrows; from Abraham and Sarah through Jacob and his wives, multiple marriages produce rivalry, jealousy, and pain. The narrator does not moralize; he simply shows us the reality. Peninnah has children. Hannah has none. The contrast is stated with spare, almost cruel brevity.

The annual pilgrimage to Shiloh is significant. Shiloh was the central sanctuary during the period of the judges, where the ark of the covenant rested and where Israel came to worship the LORD of hosts — Yahweh Sabaoth, the Lord of armies, a title that appears here for the first time in the Bible. The journey Elkanah makes year after year is an act of covenant faithfulness. He does not abandon worship because his house is sorrowful. Calvin notes that true religion does not require happy circumstances; it is precisely in affliction that the discipline of regular, corporate worship proves its worth. Elkanah brings his broken household to Shiloh, and God will meet them there.

verseByVerse.quote: On the day when Elkanah sacrificed, he would give portions to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and daughters. But to Hannah he gave a double portion, because he loved her, though the LORD had closed her womb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator offers a remarkable aside: the LORD had closed her womb. This is neither accident nor biology alone — it is divine sovereignty at work. The God who opens and closes wombs (Gen. 29:31; 30:22) has a purpose in Hannah's barrenness, even if neither she nor Elkanah can see it. R. C. Sproul notes that this attribution of Hannah's barrenness to God is not meant to be cruel but to be honest: God is the author of every circumstance, and therefore every circumstance can become the occasion for prayer.

Elkanah's double portion is a touching expression of preferential love — he cannot give Hannah what she longs for, but he gives her what he can. Yet notice: a double portion of sacrifice meat does not fill the ache for a child. Love is precious, but it cannot substitute for what God alone can give. Many of us live in the gap between what loved ones offer and what only God can supply. The double portion is grace — but it is not enough grace. Hannah will have to take her need directly to the throne.

verseByVerse.quote: And her rival used to provoke her grievously to irritate her, because the LORD had closed her womb... And Elkanah, her husband, said to her, 'Hannah, why do you weep? And why do you not eat? And why is your heart sad? Am I not more to you than ten sons?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peninnah is a relentless antagonist. Year after year, at the very moment of worship — the feast at Shiloh — she provokes Hannah until Hannah weeps and cannot eat. The cruelty is calculated: she targets the wound. And the timing is significant: it is at the house of God, during the holy feast, that Hannah's grief is most acute. Sometimes our deepest anguish surfaces in church, when joy seems most required and most absent.

Elkanah's well-meaning question — Am I not more to you than ten sons? — is the response of a loving but ultimately helpless husband. It is not wrong; it is simply insufficient. Alistair Begg remarks that Elkanah is asking Hannah to let human love substitute for divine action, and she cannot. No husband, however good, can be God. No relationship, however warm, can fill the place that belongs to the Lord. Hannah's weeping is not ingratitude toward Elkanah — it is longing directed at the only One who can answer it. Her sadness is, in its own way, a form of faith: she will not pretend satisfaction she does not feel, and she will not settle for less than what God alone can give.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hannah rises from the feast and goes alone to pray at the tabernacle, pouring out her soul to the LORD of hosts with a vow that will shape the history of Israel.
verseByVerse.theology: The vow to consecrate her son as a Nazirite (cf. Num. 6) reflects Hannah's understanding that the gift she receives is not hers to keep — it belongs to the Giver. This is the logic of all true stewardship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Nazirite vows were one of the few ways an ordinary Israelite could express total consecration to God. Now: Every child given to parents by God is a trust, not a possession — given to be given back.

verseByVerse.quote: After they had eaten and drunk in Shiloh, Hannah rose. Now Eli the priest was sitting on the seat beside the doorpost of the temple of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hannah rose. The verb is quiet but electric. She has been weeping and unable to eat. Now she gets up — not from despair but toward it; not away from her pain but into the presence of God with her pain. This is the anatomy of true prayer: not the suppression of grief but its transformation into supplication. John Calvin wrote that the Christian's prayer is the pouring of the whole soul into God's ear, and Hannah is about to demonstrate precisely that.

Eli the priest sits at the doorpost. He is present but passive, watching but not helping — a portrait of the priesthood of his day. The narrator places him there deliberately: Eli represents institutional religion doing its best, but something more is needed. Hannah will bypass the formal channels and go directly to the LORD of hosts. Her prayer will accomplish what the priesthood cannot. There is always a tension in the people of God between the institutional and the intensely personal — and 1 Samuel will trace both, showing that God works through and sometimes around the institutions he has established.

verseByVerse.quote: She was deeply distressed and prayed to the LORD and wept bitterly. And she vowed a vow and said, 'O LORD of hosts, if you will indeed look on the affliction of your servant and remember me and not forget your servant, but will give to your servant a son, then I will give him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor shall touch his head.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is one of the great prayers of the Old Testament. Notice its structure: address (O LORD of hosts), condition (if you will look… remember… not forget), petition (give me a son), and vow (I will give him to the LORD all his days). She calls herself your servant three times in a single verse — it is the posture of absolute dependence. And she addresses God as Yahweh Sabaoth, Lord of hosts, commander of the armies of heaven — as if to say: you who command legions, surely one womb is within your power.

The Nazirite vow she makes — no razor shall touch his head — echoes the language of Judges 13:5, where Samson is similarly dedicated before birth. But Hannah's Samuel will outshine Samson: where Samson's gifts were physical and he spent them selfishly, Samuel's gifts will be spiritual and he will spend them wholly for God's people. The vow also contains an extraordinary act of surrender: I will give him to the LORD. She asks for a son with the intention of giving him back. This is the logic of all true Christian stewardship, and it prefigures the Father who gave his only Son, and that Son who gave himself completely for his people.

verseByVerse.quote: As she continued praying before the LORD, Eli observed her mouth. Hannah was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard. Therefore Eli took her to be a drunken woman... But Hannah answered, 'No, my lord, I am a woman troubled in spirit.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eli's misreading of Hannah is both comic and painful. He sees a woman with moving lips and no audible voice and concludes she is drunk. His rebuke — put away your wine — is a stunning failure of pastoral discernment. Here is the high priest of Israel, unable to recognize genuine prayer when it is happening in front of him. Calvin finds the irony sharp: the man appointed to hear Israel's prayers cannot distinguish prayer from drunkenness. It is a quiet indictment of the spiritual state of the Elide priesthood — and a foretaste of what chapters 2–4 will make explicit.

Hannah's response is dignified, specific, and theologically precise: I am a woman troubled in spirit… I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD. She does not bow to Eli's authority when his authority is wrong; she corrects him gently and truthfully. And Eli, to his credit, receives the correction and blesses her: Go in peace, and the God of Israel grant your petition. Hannah's immediate response — she ate, and her face was no longer sad — is not evidence that the prayer was answered (it hasn't been yet); it is evidence that she believed. She cast her burden on the Lord and left it there. That act of faith, not the birth itself, is the first miracle of the chapter.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD remembers Hannah; Samuel is born, named 'asked of God,' nursed, and then brought to Shiloh to be left with Eli — the vow fulfilled with a whole heart.
verseByVerse.theology: The name Samuel (asked of God / heard by God) seals the theology of the chapter: prayer is heard, answered, and the gift is surrendered back. The structure anticipates Abraham and Isaac on Moriah.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Weaning in the ancient world took two to three years — Hannah had Samuel for a precious but brief season before giving him up. Now: Every act of costly giving back to God — a child, a career, a comfort — echoes Hannah's surrender at Shiloh.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elkanah knew Hannah his wife, and the LORD remembered her. And in due time Hannah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Samuel, for she said, 'I have asked for him from the LORD.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD remembered Hannah — a phrase that in Hebrew (zakar) carries the force of active, saving attention. God does not merely recall Hannah; he acts on her behalf. The same word is used of God remembering Noah in the ark (Gen. 8:1), remembering Rachel and opening her womb (Gen. 30:22), and remembering his covenant with Abraham (Ex. 2:24). To be remembered by God is to be rescued by God. This is covenantal language: Hannah is not forgotten; she is God's own.

The name Samuel is given a folk etymology — sha'ul me'el, asked of God — though the Hebrew name actually sounds more like Saul (sha'ul). Some scholars think this hints at the larger story: the one asked for will anoint and then reject the one named Saul. But more immediately, the name is a permanent testimony. Every time anyone speaks Samuel's name, they announce that prayer is answered, God hears, and the impossible yields to grace. His very existence is a sermon. Sinclair Ferguson writes that Samuel's birth is Israel's hope arriving in the most unassuming form — a baby in the hill country — which is precisely how all of God's great deliverances begin.

verseByVerse.quote: And she said to Elkanah her husband, 'As soon as the child is weaned, I will bring him, so that he may appear in the presence of the LORD and dwell there forever.' ... For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition that I made to him. Therefore I have lent him to the LORD. As long as he lives, he is lent to the LORD.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hannah waits until Samuel is weaned — perhaps two or three years — and then, with a generous sacrifice (three bulls, an ephah of flour, a skin of wine), she brings him to Shiloh and presents him to Eli. What follows is one of the most emotionally charged scenes in all of Scripture: a mother handing her young child to an old priest and walking away. She has prayed for this child with tears and received him with joy, and now she gives him up with worship.

The word translated lent (sha'al) echoes the name Samuel throughout: I asked… he granted… I am lending him back. This is not reluctant obedience; it is whole-hearted surrender. The Puritan Thomas Boston wrote that the highest use of a gift is to return it to the Giver, consecrated. Hannah understands what most of us resist: the child is not hers. She received him as a trust, and now she discharges the trust. Her action prefigures Abraham on Moriah, and both together cast a long shadow toward Calvary — where the Father gives his own Son, not borrowing him back. Hannah's worship here (the chapter ends with her worshipping, v. 28) is the appropriate response to grace: everything given, everything surrendered, everything received as gift.

1.theology:
The Sovereignty of God Over Human Barrenness. The deliberate statement that the LORD had closed her womb (v. 5) anchors the chapter's theology: God is sovereign over the very biology that causes Hannah's grief. This is not a comfortable doctrine, but it is a sustaining one. If God has closed, God can open. If God has withheld, God can give. Hannah's prayer is not wishful thinking; it is faith engaging the God who holds all things in his hand. R. C. Sproul insists that the sovereignty of God is the only foundation on which genuine prayer makes sense: we do not pray to change God's mind but to engage God's will — and sometimes, as here, God's will is to wait for the prayer before giving the gift.

Prayer as the Soul Poured Out. Hannah's prayer in verses 10–11 — wordless to human ears, heard perfectly by God — models what Alistair Begg calls 'the prayer that cannot be dressed up.' It has no formal liturgy, no impressive rhetoric. It is grief becoming petition. The LORD hears what Eli cannot discern, which is itself a statement about the nature of God: he reads hearts, not performances. The chapter thus issues an implicit invitation: bring the prayer you cannot articulate, the need that has no clean words, and trust the LORD of hosts to hear.
1.examples:
Then: In ancient Israel, barrenness was social death. A woman without children had no security, no standing, no future. Hannah's grief was compounded by Peninnah's cruelty and the silence of heaven. Yet she did not abandon worship or turn to false gods — she brought her anguish to Shiloh, year after year, until the answer came.

Now: The chapter speaks directly to everyone carrying an unanswered prayer — an infertility journey, a prodigal child, a chronic illness, a longing that will not quiet. Hannah's example does not promise that God will give what we ask; it promises that God hears what we ask and that faith can live in the gap between petition and answer. And her surrender of Samuel after receiving him is a model for how we hold all gifts loosely: children, health, relationships, gifting — received from God, held with open hands, given back when he asks.

2.title: The Horn of His Anointed
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And Hannah prayed and said, 'My heart exults in the LORD; my horn is exalted in the LORD. My mouth derides my enemies, because I rejoice in your salvation. <sup>2</sup>There is none holy like the LORD: for there is none besides you; there is no rock like our God.' <sup>10</sup>The adversaries of the LORD shall be broken to pieces; against them he will thunder in heaven. The LORD will judge the ends of the earth; he will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed. (ESV)
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is built around a stunning contrast. It opens with Hannah's incomparable song — a canticle of sovereign grace that Mary will echo fourteen centuries later in the Magnificat — and then immediately descends into the sordid moral ruin of Eli's sons. The structure is deliberate: the new thing God is doing (Samuel, the anointed, the coming king) is being born at the very moment the old order is rotting from within. Hannah sees it before anyone else does, because she has prayed her way into the heart of God.

Hannah's song in verses 1–10 is the theological summit of 1 Samuel and one of the programmatic texts of all Scripture. Its themes — the reversal of human status, the humbling of the proud and the exaltation of the lowly, the sovereign God who kills and makes alive, raises up and brings down — are the grammar of the gospel. And its final verse, he will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed (v. 10), is the first appearance of the word mashiach in its eschatological sense: the book of 1 Samuel opens by pointing, however dimly, to the Christ.

Against this height, the narrative plunges: Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are named worthless men who did not know the LORD (v. 12). Their sins are specific and audacious — stealing the sacrificial meat by force, lying with the women who served at the tabernacle entrance. They turn worship into appetite. And Eli's response — too little, too late — seals the judgment. The man of God's announcement in verses 27–36 is one of the most solemn prophetic speeches in the Old Testament: the Elide priesthood is ended, and God will raise up a faithful priest.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Hannah's Song: The Magnificat of the Old Testament
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hannah's prayer of praise overflows into a canticle that surveys the whole economy of divine grace: the reversal of fortunes, the sovereignty of God over life and death, and the coming of the anointed king.
verseByVerse.theology: The song moves from personal experience (vv. 1–3) to cosmic theology (vv. 4–8) to eschatological hope (vv. 9–10). Hannah's womb was the microscope through which she saw the pattern of all God's redemptive work.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Hannah sings in the shadow of her own answered prayer; the song is simultaneously personal testimony and prophetic vision. Now: The pattern — humbling the proud, exalting the humble — is the shape of all gospel work, and the church sings it whenever it gathers.

verseByVerse.quote: My heart exults in the LORD; my horn is exalted in the LORD. My mouth derides my enemies... There is none holy like the LORD... Talk no more so very proudly, let not arrogance come from your mouth, for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hannah's song begins in the first person and immediately moves to the character of God. This is the mark of mature praise: it does not stay long on personal experience but uses personal experience as a launch point for theological declaration. My horn is exalted — the horn is the OT image of strength and dignity; the barren woman who was taunted by her rival now stands with her head high, not because she has won a social contest, but because the LORD has acted. Her exaltation is entirely derivative: in the LORD, in your salvation.

Verses 2–3 are a direct rebuke of the proud — and while Hannah may have Peninnah in mind, the application is cosmic. Talk no more so very proudly is addressed to all who depend on their own strength, fertility, wisdom, or standing. The LORD is a God of knowledge (de'ot, literally 'knowledges' — the plural of intensity): he sees through every pretension. By him actions are weighed. This is Hannah's answer to Peninnah's provocation and to every human arrogance: the scales of God are calibrated differently from human scales, and in the end, they alone matter. John Calvin finds in these verses a summary of what he calls the theology of the cross: the way up is down, and the way to strength is through acknowledged weakness.

verseByVerse.quote: The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble bind on strength. Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread, but those who were hungry have ceased to hunger... He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap to make them sit with princes...
verseByVerse.commentary:
These verses trace the great reversal that is the signature of God's way in the world. In quick, almost breathless pairs, Hannah sets down the pattern: mighty/feeble, full/hungry, barren/mother, dead/alive, poor/princes. Each inversion is not a social program but a theological statement: the God of Israel is not captive to the status quo. He kills and makes alive (v. 6 — an astonishing, almost alarming claim); he brings down to Sheol and raises up. The same God who closed Hannah's womb has now opened it, and this act is a window into the very nature of divine sovereignty.

Verse 8's cosmic sweep — the pillars of the earth are the LORD's, and on them he has set the world — grounds the social reversals in creation theology. The God who reverses human fortunes is the God who made and upholds the world. Tim Keller observes that Hannah's song teaches a radically different anthropology than any the world offers: human dignity does not come from achievement, fertility, beauty, or power, but from being created and upheld by this God who delights to lift the poor from the dust. This is the foundation of what Keller calls 'the dignity of the lowly' — a dignity that no Peninnah can take away and no barrenness can erase.

Mary, when she receives the announcement of the incarnation, will sing almost these exact words in Luke 1:46–55. The Magnificat is not a new composition; it is Hannah's song remembered and deepened, applied now to the greatest reversal of all — the Word made flesh, the eternal Son becoming a vulnerable infant in a Bethlehem stable, the exaltation of the lowly reaching its apex in the incarnation.

verseByVerse.quote: He will guard the feet of his faithful ones, but the wicked shall be cut off in darkness, for not by might shall a man prevail. The adversaries of the LORD shall be broken to pieces; against them he will thunder in heaven. The LORD will judge the ends of the earth; he will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The song ends with its most electrifying lines. He will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed — the word anointed here is meshicho, his mashiach, his Christ. This is the first appearance in Scripture of the anointed one in a clearly eschatological and royal sense. Hannah could not have known what she was saying in its fullness; she was praying for the coming Israelite king, and she may have had Samuel's future role or David's in mind. But the Spirit of God was doing what he always does in the prophets: carrying the human word further than the speaker's intention into the deep purposes of God.

R. C. Sproul notes that every subsequent use of mashiach in the OT — culminating in Daniel 9:25–26 — draws from this stream. Hannah's song, born from barrenness and answered prayer in the hill country of Ephraim, becomes the seedbed of messianic expectation. And the first hearers of Luke's Gospel, who knew their Scriptures, would have felt the tremor of recognition when Mary sang in Luke 1: this is Hannah's song made flesh, the horn exalted not in a king on an earthly throne but in the eternal Son who rules from a cross and a resurrection throne. Not by might shall a man prevail — and the mightiest victory in history was won by the One who had nowhere to lay his head.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–17 — The Corruption of the Priesthood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The narrative descends from Hannah's exalted theology to the sordid reality of Eli's sons: Hophni and Phinehas are 'worthless men who did not know the LORD,' stealing sacrificial meat and treating worship as a means of personal gain.
verseByVerse.theology: The contrast between Hannah's song and Hophni/Phinehas's behavior is the theological engine of the chapter: where Hannah poured out her life before God, they pour out the holy things for themselves. The failure of institutional religion creates the very crisis that Samuel will be raised up to address.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Priestly corruption in Israel was a capital offense — the priests represented God to the people and distorted that representation for personal gain. Now: Whenever the church's leaders treat ministry as an opportunity for personal advantage — money, power, reputation — they commit the same sin.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the sons of Eli were worthless men. They did not know the LORD. The custom of the priests with the people was that when any man offered sacrifice... the servant would come while the meat was boiling and thrust a fork... and all that the fork brought up the priest would take for himself... thus the sin of the young men was very great in the sight of the LORD, for the men treated the offering of the LORD with contempt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three words define Hophni and Phinehas at the outset: worthless men who did not know the LORD. In Hebrew, bene beliyya'al — sons of Belial, sons of worthlessness, later a name for Satan himself in the NT. The diagnosis is theological before it is behavioral: they did not know the LORD. Their theft of the sacrificial portions and their sexual sin with the tabernacle women (v. 22) are symptoms of a prior disease: they have no living relationship with the God they serve. They use the sacred machinery of worship without the sacred reality. This is what Sinclair Ferguson calls 'professional religion' — the form of godliness without its power (2 Tim. 3:5).

The mechanics of their theft are spelled out with damning specificity. Before the fat had been burned — which belonged to God by law (Lev. 3:16) — they demanded raw meat. When rebuked, they threatened force. The narrative lingers on the detail to make clear: this is not mere carelessness. It is contempt. They treat the offering of the LORD with contempt (v. 17). The same Hebrew root (baza') will be used of Saul's half-hearted obedience in chapter 15. Contempt for God's instructions, however dressed in religious attire, is a recurring sin that 1 Samuel anatomizes with ruthless clarity.

verseByVerse.quote: Samuel was ministering before the LORD, a boy clothed with a linen ephod. And his mother used to make for him a little robe and take it to him each year when she went up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against the darkness of Hophni and Phinehas, the narrator inserts Samuel twice in this chapter (vv. 11, 18) with the same quiet phrase: ministering before the LORD. The contrast is deliberate and instructive. Where the sons of Eli use the holy garments as costumes for exploitation, Samuel wears the linen ephod as a genuine servant. Where they take, he serves. Where they are named and shamed, he is named and blessed.

The detail of Hannah's annual robe is one of the most tender in all of Scripture. A mother who has surrendered her son to God's service makes him a little robe every year — growing with him, a tangible expression of continuing love across the distance. She does not disappear from his life; she finds new forms of presence within her vow. And God honors this: Eli blesses Elkanah and Hannah, and the LORD gives them three more sons and two daughters (v. 21). The one who gives back receives more than they surrendered. This is not a prosperity formula; it is the pattern of grace: the open hand is filled, the closed fist starves.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Eli was very old, and he kept hearing all that his sons were doing to all Israel, and how they lay with the women who were serving at the entrance to the tent of meeting. And he said to them, 'Why do you do such things?...' But they would not listen to the voice of their father, for it was the will of the LORD to put them to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eli's rebuke of his sons is the most damning statement of his own failure. He knows. He has heard everything. And all he offers is Why do you do such things? — a rhetorical question that carries no authority, imposes no discipline, demands no repentance. As the high priest, Eli had the authority to remove his sons from office; instead, he asks them why they behave badly and lets them continue. He honors his sons above God (2:29) — the charge that the man of God will bring against him explicitly.

The narrator adds a chilling theological note: it was the will of the LORD to put them to death. This is not an excuse for Hophni and Phinehas — their sin is their own — but a declaration of divine judgment already operative. They have crossed the threshold of what Calvin calls 'judicial hardening': their refusal to listen to their father is itself the evidence that God has determined their end. The same pattern will repeat with Saul in chapter 15, and its New Testament counterpart is Romans 1:24–28. There is a fearful patience in God that eventually exhausts itself, and when it does, the sinner's own refusal becomes the instrument of judgment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–36 — The Prophecy Against the House of Eli
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An unnamed man of God delivers a devastating oracle against Eli and his house: the priesthood that should have honored God has despised him, and it will be stripped away. A faithful priest is promised in its place.
verseByVerse.theology: The prophecy moves from accusation (vv. 27–29) to sentence (vv. 30–34) to promise (vv. 35–36). Its structure mirrors the entire message of 1 Samuel: judgment on the old order, promise of the new. The 'faithful priest' points ultimately to Christ, the one high priest who always does what is pleasing to the Father.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Elide priesthood ends at Shiloh's fall (ch. 4) and is finally displaced when Solomon removes Abiathar (1 Kings 2:27), fulfilling this word. Now: Every institution that treats God's glory as a means to human ends will eventually be displaced by the faithful priest — Christ himself — who alone always honors the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: And there came a man of God to Eli and said to him, 'Thus says the LORD, Did I indeed reveal myself to the house of your father when they were in Egypt?... Why then do you scorn my sacrifices and my offerings that I commanded for my dwelling, and honor your sons above me by fattening yourselves on the choicest parts of every offering of my people Israel?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The unnamed man of God begins with covenant history — God's original call and revelation to the house of Levi in Egypt — to make clear what is at stake in Eli's failure. The priesthood is not a human institution that God merely permits; it is a divine appointment rooted in the Exodus. To dishonor the priesthood is to dishonor the God who instituted it. And the specific charge against Eli is piercing: you honor your sons above me. Eli is guilty not of the same sins as his sons but of the greater sin of preferring family peace to God's honor.

This is the pastoral failure that reappears across church history: the leader who knows that something is deeply wrong but will not act because it will cost too much. Eli loved his sons more than he loved God's glory. The result is that he loses both: God removes the priesthood from his line, and his sons die on the same day (4:11). Alistair Begg observes that the failure to exercise godly discipline — in families, in churches — is never neutral. It always has a cost, and the cost is almost always borne by others.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore the LORD, the God of Israel, declares: '...far be it from me, for those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed... And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall do according to what is in my heart and in my mind.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sentence against the house of Eli contains one of the great theological axioms of the Old Testament: those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed. This is not a commercial transaction; it is a covenant principle. The God who gave the priesthood to Aaron's line will also take it away when that line dishonors him. Divine appointment does not guarantee divine protection if the appointment is used for self-service.

But the prophecy does not end in judgment. It ends in promise: I will raise up for myself a faithful priest. In the immediate context, this points to Samuel and then to Zadok (1 Kings 2). But the fuller horizon — which the NT writers will read clearly — is Christ. Hebrews 2:17 describes Jesus as a merciful and faithful high priest, and the entire argument of Hebrews 7–10 is that Christ is the faithful priest who does what is in the heart and mind of the Father, who offers not the fat of bulls but himself, who serves not for his own benefit but for ours. Every priestly failure in the OT — Eli, Hophni, Phinehas, and the long sorry line of corrupt priests — is a photographic negative of the one Priest who never fails, never takes, never honors himself above the Father.

2.theology:
The Grammar of Grace: Reversal. Hannah's song articulates the principle that governs all of God's redemptive work: the last shall be first, the barren shall be fruitful, the hungry shall be filled, the poor shall be lifted from the dust. This is not mere sentimentality but the revealed character of the sovereign God. Tim Keller argues that this reversal theology is the lens through which all of history must be read, and it reaches its climax in the cross — where the almighty One becomes the crucified One, and the crucified One becomes the exalted One. The Magnificat in Luke 1 is Hannah's song transposed into its ultimate key.

Knowing God vs. Serving God. Hophni and Phinehas did not know the LORD (v. 12) even while serving in his house. The most dangerous form of unbelief is the kind dressed in religious clothing. John MacArthur notes that the sons of Eli are a warning to every person who performs religious duties without personal knowledge of God: ritual without relationship is not merely useless — it is dangerous, because it produces the illusion of standing with God while the reality is contempt.
2.examples:
Then: The contrast between Hannah's joyful surrender and Eli's sons' grasping contempt defined the spiritual crisis of the judges era. Israel's worship had become a transaction managed by corrupt brokers. The new thing God was doing — Samuel, the anointed, the coming king — was being born precisely in the wreckage of the old system.

Now: The chapter addresses every church: Is our worship an act of whole-hearted surrender to God, or have we turned it into a platform for our own benefit? And it addresses every individual: Do I know God, or merely serve him? The sons of Eli are the cautionary tale; Hannah is the model. The difference is not intelligence or education or even behavior — it is the posture of the heart before the LORD of hosts.

3.title: The Word of the LORD Was Rare
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the young man Samuel was ministering to the LORD under Eli. And the word of the LORD was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision. <sup>10</sup>And the LORD came and stood, calling as at other times, 'Samuel! Samuel!' And Samuel said, 'Speak, for your servant hears.' (ESV)
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is one of the most perfectly constructed narratives in the entire Bible. Its dramatic tension — the repeated calling in the night, the repeated misidentification, the growing recognition — is almost cinematic in its pacing. But its theological weight is enormous: in a time when the word of the LORD was rare, God breaks his silence and speaks to a child, bypassing the high priest to deliver a message of devastating judgment.

The chapter opens with a double diagnosis of the spiritual state of Israel: the word of the LORD was rare, and there was no frequent vision (v. 1). This is famine of a different kind — not bread but the word of God (cf. Amos 8:11). The lamps in the tabernacle were going out (v. 3) — a detail both literal and symbolic: the spiritual light of Israel was guttering. And Eli, whose eyes had grown dim (v. 2), could not see the dawning revelation.

Samuel's commission as a prophet is bound up with the word he receives — and dread the word he must deliver. The whole house of Eli will fall, and nothing — no sacrifice, no offering — can atone for it. Samuel's faithfulness in delivering this word to Eli, and Eli's resigned acceptance of it (It is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him, v. 18), form the moral center of the chapter.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Darkness Before the Dawn
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three details set the scene: the word of the LORD is rare, Eli's eyes are dim, and the lamp of God is going out in the tabernacle. The spiritual state of Israel has never been lower — which is exactly when God acts.
verseByVerse.theology: The rarity of divine revelation is itself a form of judgment on a generation that has treated God's word with contempt (2:17, 2:29). Yet it also creates the moment for a new beginning. God's silence is always purposeful.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Without prophet or vision, Israel had to navigate solely by the law Moses gave — which they had largely abandoned. Now: The church in any era of spiritual decline feels the famine of genuine prophetic preaching; the answer is always the same — a new, costly call to faithful hearing.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision. At that time Eli, whose eyesight had begun to grow dim so that he could not see, was lying down in his own place. The lamp of God had not yet gone out, and Samuel was lying down in the temple of the LORD, where the ark of God was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The phrase the word of the LORD was rare is the saddest sentence in the book up to this point. The Hebrew word for rare (yaqar) means precious, costly, scarce — it describes something so valuable it is almost never seen. In a nation supposed to live by the revelation of God, his voice has become a rarity. This is not God's failure but Israel's: a generation that treated the LORD's offerings with contempt (2:17) and whose priests did not know him (2:12) had produced spiritual deafness in the land.

Eli's physical blindness mirrors the spiritual blindness of the age. His eyes are dim — and he will spend the rest of his story unable to see clearly, physically or spiritually. But there is a counter-detail: the lamp of God had not yet gone out. In the tabernacle, the golden lampstand was to burn through the night and be tended each morning (Ex. 27:20–21); by the time of Samuel's call, it was burning down but had not yet gone out. The detail is almost unbearably tender: in the darkness of Israel's spiritual decline, the last light is still burning, and a boy is sleeping near the ark of God. The dawn is about to come from the most unexpected direction.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD called Samuel, and he said, 'Here I am!' and ran to Eli and said, 'Here I am, for you called me.' But he said, 'I did not call; lie down again.' So he went and lay down. And the LORD called again, 'Samuel!'... (This happened three times.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The threefold calling and the threefold misidentification is more than narrative charm — it is a theological portrait of a soul learning to hear God. Samuel, for all his genuine devotion, does not yet recognize the voice of the LORD: Samuel did not yet know the LORD, and the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him (v. 7). This is not a mark against Samuel; it is a mark of his situation. He has been faithful in service, but the experiential knowledge of God's voice is new.

Eli's slowness to recognize what is happening is equally instructive. He has to be told three times before he understands that God is calling the boy. This is the same Eli who, at his best, could bless Hannah after misjudging her. He is not a bad man; he is a man whose spiritual sensitivity has been dulled by years of compromise and accommodation. He knows enough, finally, to instruct Samuel correctly: Speak, LORD, for your servant hears (v. 9). In the end, Eli gives Samuel the right words even if he himself has lost the capacity to hear them. Sometimes the church's greatest service is to pass on to the next generation the means of encountering God even when the current generation has grown too dim to see him clearly.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD stands before Samuel and delivers the full weight of the judgment against Eli's house — a judgment so severe that no sacrifice or offering can avert it. Samuel must hear and then deliver this terrible word.
verseByVerse.theology: The severity of the judgment is proportionate to the gravity of the sin: Eli's sons blasphemed God (v. 13, LXX reads 'cursed God'), and Eli refused to restrain them. The inability of sacrifice to atone for willful, knowing contempt anticipates Hebrews 10:26–27.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Israelite sacrificial system was designed for inadvertent sins and sins of weakness, not for high-handed contempt of God (Num. 15:30–31). Now: There is a category of spiritual hardness that moves beyond the reach of ordinary remedies; the answer is not more religion but genuine repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD came and stood, calling as at other times, 'Samuel! Samuel!' And Samuel said, 'Speak, for your servant hears.' Then the LORD said to Samuel, 'Behold, I am about to do a thing in Israel at which the two ears of everyone who hears it will tingle... For I have told him that I am about to punish his house forever, for the iniquity that he knew, because his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God stood before Samuel — the Hebrew suggests a theophanic presence, an actual appearance that makes this not merely an auditory experience but a direct divine encounter. And the word Samuel receives is shattering: at which the two ears of everyone who hears it will tingle. This is the Bible's description of news so terrible it produces a physical sensation, a ringing in the ears of shock. The judgment against Eli is not simply removal from office; it is the permanent, irreversible punishment of his entire line.

The specific charge is piercing: his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them. The verb translated blaspheming (or 'cursing' in some MSS) is qalal — to treat as light, to despise. They treated the holy things lightly; Eli treated their treatment lightly. The compounded contempt is what makes it irredeemable. And the sentence is explicit: the iniquity of Eli's house shall not be atoned for by sacrifice or offering forever. There are sins for which the sacrificial system provides no remedy — not because God is unjust, but because those sins represent a fundamental rejection of the covenant relationship that sacrifice was designed to restore. As Hebrews 10:26 will say: if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins.

verseByVerse.quote: Samuel lay until morning; then he opened the doors of the house of the LORD. And Samuel was afraid to tell the vision to Eli. But Eli called Samuel and said, 'Samuel, my son.' And he said, 'Here I am.' And Eli said, 'What was it that he told you? Do not hide it from me... It is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samuel's fear is profoundly human. He has just received from God a word of devastating judgment against the man who raised him, the father-figure of his young life. Telling Eli will be one of the hardest things he ever does. Alistair Begg notes that the first test of a prophet is not whether God will speak to him, but whether he will speak for God when it costs him something. Samuel passes this test at dawn, on his first day as a prophet.

Eli's question — Do not hide it from me; may God do so to you if you hide anything from me — is strangely dignified. He already suspects what the message contains. And his response to hearing it — It is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him — is a moment of genuine, if tragic, faith. Not repentance (which might have come sooner and done something); not rebellion; but resigned submission to divine sovereignty. Calvin finds in Eli's response a broken but real acknowledgment that God is just. The old priest cannot undo what his passivity has set in motion, but he can bow before the God who judges righteously. It is too little, too late — but it is real.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD was with Samuel, let none of his words fall to the ground, and all Israel recognized him as a prophet — the first genuine prophet since Moses.
verseByVerse.theology: The validation of a prophet in Israel was the fulfillment of his words (Deut. 18:22). Samuel's establishment is the establishment of the prophetic office in a new and decisive form — pointing toward the great Prophet to come (Deut. 18:15).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: From Dan to Beersheba — the whole land — recognized Samuel's prophetic call. The authority of the prophet was national, not local. Now: The call to speak God's word faithfully is always costly and always confirmed not by human appointment but by God's own validation.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel grew, and the LORD was with him and let none of his words fall to the ground. And all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established as a prophet of the LORD. And the LORD appeared again at Shiloh, for the LORD revealed himself to Samuel at Shiloh by the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three compressed verses announce a new era. The LORD was with him — the covenant formula of divine accompaniment that marks every true servant of God, from Joseph to Joshua to Jesus himself (Acts 10:38). Let none of his words fall to the ground — this is the test of Deuteronomy 18:22 applied and passed: when the prophet speaks, it happens. Every word that comes from Samuel's mouth will be fulfilled, because it is not Samuel's word but God's word through him.

The final verse is almost offhand in its magnitude: the LORD revealed himself to Samuel at Shiloh by the word of the LORD. The word was rare; now it is regular. The vision was absent; now it has returned. The lamp was going out; now it burns again. And it burns through a boy who was willing to say, Speak, for your servant hears, and who, when he heard a hard word, had the courage to deliver it. This is the pattern of all prophetic ministry — and ultimately of the ministry of Christ himself, who is the Word made flesh, the prophet who is himself the revelation, in whom all the words of God find their Yes and Amen (2 Cor. 1:20).

3.theology:
The Word That Will Not Fall. The great theme of chapter 3 is the relationship between God's word and God's action. When the LORD speaks through Samuel, none of his words fall to the ground (v. 19) — they land, they happen, they accomplish what they announce. This is the character of divine speech from Genesis 1 onward: God speaks and it is so. The rarity of the word in Samuel's day was itself a judgment; its restoration through Samuel is a mercy. And the NT picks up this theme definitively in Hebrews 1:1–2: Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son. Samuel is a herald; Christ is the message.

Learning to Hear God's Voice. Samuel did not recognize God's voice on the first call, or the second, or the third. This is not an embarrassment to be explained away; it is an encouragement for every believer who finds the practice of hearing God difficult. The discipline of prayer, the reading of Scripture, the wisdom of mature brothers and sisters — these are the Eli-equivalents who help us identify the divine voice. And the posture once recognized — Speak, Lord, for your servant hears — is the pattern of all sanctification: the willingness to receive what God says, even when it is hard.
3.examples:
Then: Israel in Samuel's day had virtually no access to fresh prophetic word — they were living on the stored light of the Mosaic revelation, administered by a corrupt priesthood. The arrival of Samuel as a true prophet was a national rescue. Without the word of God, a people cannot navigate, cannot repent, cannot worship truly.

Now: The chapter speaks to every preacher and to every congregation. Preachers: will you hear the hard word and deliver it faithfully, even when it costs you the affection of those you love? Congregations: will you train yourselves to hear God's voice in Scripture, or will you sleep through the calling? The lamp of God has not gone out — the canon is complete, the Spirit is given, and Christ the Word dwells among his people. The question is whether we, like Samuel, will lie near the ark and say, Speak, for your servant hears.

4.title: Ichabod: The Glory Has Departed
4.text: <sup>21</sup>And she named the child Ichabod, saying, 'The glory has departed from Israel!' because the ark of God had been captured and because of her father-in-law and her husband. <sup>22</sup>And she said, 'The glory has departed from Israel, for the ark of God has been captured.' (ESV)
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is one of the most catastrophic chapters in the Old Testament. In the span of a few verses, Israel loses thirty thousand soldiers, the ark of God is captured by the Philistines, Eli's two sons die on the same day in fulfillment of the man of God's prophecy, Eli himself falls from his seat and dies, and a dying woman names her child Ichabod — the glory has departed. Everything Samuel warned about has happened, and it has happened with terrifying speed.

The theological crisis at the heart of the chapter is Israel's fatal misunderstanding of the ark. When the first battle goes badly, the elders of Israel decide to bring the ark from Shiloh to the battlefield, reasoning that the physical presence of the ark guarantees divine help. They have turned the symbol of God's presence into a talisman, a magic object whose power can be deployed regardless of the spiritual condition of those deploying it. They shout so loudly the ground shakes — and then they lose anyway. The ark is not a rabbit's foot. The presence of God cannot be manipulated by the merely religious.

Yet the chapter does not end in pure despair. The name Ichabod — no glory, or where is the glory? — is simultaneously a lament and a question. The glory has departed; but God is not finished. The ark's journey into Philistine territory (chapters 5–6) will demonstrate that the Lord of hosts does not need Israel's army to vindicate his honor.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Ark Brought to Battle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel loses the first battle and draws the catastrophic conclusion that the ark's physical presence will guarantee victory. The Philistines hear the ark has arrived and are initially terrified — but they fight anyway.
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's error is the perennial sin of confusing the sign with the reality, the symbol with the God it represents. The ark was the throne of the invisible God; they treat it as a portable deity they can deploy at will.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel had precedent for the ark's presence in battle — the Jordan crossing, the Jericho conquest. But those victories came through obedience, not mechanical deployment. Now: The church falls into the same error whenever it deploys religious forms — services, sacraments, programs — as if the forms themselves secure God's blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of Samuel came to all Israel. Now Israel went out to battle against the Philistines... Israel was defeated before the Philistines, who killed about four thousand men on the field of battle. And when the people came to the camp, the elders of Israel said, 'Why has the LORD defeated us today before the Philistines? Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD here from Shiloh, that it may come among us and save us from the power of our enemies.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders ask the right question — Why has the LORD defeated us? — and arrive at the wrong answer. The right answer was staring them in the face: the corruption of the priesthood, the contempt for God's offerings, the moral and spiritual decay of the nation. But instead of asking what must we repent of, they ask what must we deploy. R. C. Sproul observes that this is the characteristic move of religion without relationship: when things go wrong, reach for the religious resource rather than the relational reality.

The ark was the most sacred object in Israel — the chest covered in gold, with the mercy seat between the cherubim, where God's presence dwelt in a unique way. It had been present at great victories. But its presence was never the cause of those victories; the LORD of hosts was. The elders have confused the container with the content. They want the ark, but they do not want the God of the ark — or rather, they want him on their terms, as a guarantee of military success, without the prior requirement of covenant obedience. Sinclair Ferguson writes that this is a form of practical atheism dressed in religious clothing: using God's name and God's symbols while ignoring God's demands.

verseByVerse.quote: So the people sent to Shiloh and brought from there the ark of the covenant of the LORD of hosts, who is enthroned on the cherubim. And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of God. When the ark of the covenant of the LORD came into the camp, all Israel gave a mighty shout, so that the earth resounded... But the Philistines were afraid, for they said, 'Gods have come into the camp.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrative detail that Hophni and Phinehas accompanied the ark is charged with irony. These are the men whose sins have caused the divine judgment; they are now the custodians of the divine symbol. The very men who were bringing God's curse on Israel are now carrying his ark into battle. No wonder the ark does not function as Israel expects.

The Philistines' reaction is theologically fascinating. They know Israel's history — the plagues, the Exodus, the destruction of Og and Sihon. They are afraid, genuinely afraid. And then they talk themselves into fighting anyway: be strong and be men, O Philistines, lest you become slaves to Hebrews as they have been to you (v. 9). They recognize the danger and choose to fight through it. There is a dark courage in the Philistines here that shames Israel: Israel shouts and retreats; the Philistines are terrified and advance. The battle will be won not by the nation with the right religious symbol but by the nation with the greater determination. God does not guarantee victory to those who carry his ark; he guarantees his presence to those who walk in obedience to his covenant.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–18 — The Death of Eli's Sons and Eli Himself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second battle is a catastrophe: thirty thousand fall, the ark is taken, Hophni and Phinehas are killed. A Benjaminite messenger carries the news to Shiloh, and the report kills Eli at the gate.
verseByVerse.theology: The three deaths — Hophni, Phinehas, Eli — happen on the same day, fulfilling the man of God's prophecy (2:34). Divine judgments, when they come, are precise and complete. The sign to Eli was not merely a warning but a prediction.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The loss of the ark was the theological equivalent of national death — the departure of the divine presence from Israel's midst. Now: The departure of God's presence from a church — marked by loss of genuine word, genuine worship, genuine holiness — is the greatest possible catastrophe, far worse than any external threat.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated, and they fled, every man to his home. And there was a very great slaughter, for there fell of Israel thirty thousand foot soldiers. And the ark of God was captured, and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The brevity of the narration is devastating. Thirty thousand men, the ark taken, the two sons of the high priest dead — three lines. The narrator does not slow down to mourn; the swift, compressed reporting mirrors the swiftness of the catastrophe itself. There is no last-minute rescue, no divine intervention, no miracle. God permits his own ark to be captured by pagan enemies. This is the most disturbing theological fact of the chapter, and it will be addressed in chapters 5–6: the ark's capture is not God's defeat; it is God's peculiar sovereignty choosing to vindicate himself in a way Israel could never have imagined.

The deaths of Hophni and Phinehas are the precise fulfillment of the sign given in 2:34: and both of your sons, Hophni and Phinehas, shall die on the same day. The sign has come. There is a terrible momentum to prophecy: once spoken by the LORD, it will not be deflected. John Calvin writes that the fulfillment of judgment prophecies, though terrible, is actually a ground of trust: the God who keeps his threatening words is the same God who keeps his promises of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: A man of Benjamin ran from the battle line and came to Shiloh the same day, with his clothes torn and with dirt on his head. When he arrived, Eli was sitting on his seat by the road watching, for his heart trembled for the ark of God... When he mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell over backward from his seat by the side of the gate, and his neck was broken and he died, for the man was old and heavy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eli has been sitting by the road, trembling. Not for his sons — the narrator notes this carefully — but for the ark. It is perhaps the most sympathetic thing we ever hear about Eli: whatever his failures as a father and a priest, he knew enough to fear for the ark of God. And the news that kills him is precisely the news about the ark. His sons' deaths barely register; when he hears the ark is taken, he falls and dies.

Eli dies at ninety-eight, having judged Israel forty years. His death is neither heroic nor shameful — it is simply the end of an era that has been ending for years. He sat in his seat while his sons desecrated the tabernacle; he falls from his seat when the tabernacle's glory departs. The physical fall is an enactment of the spiritual fall of his house. Alistair Begg observes that Eli is the Bible's portrait of a man who knew better than he did — who had genuine faith and genuine love for the things of God but who lacked the moral courage to act on that knowledge. He ends not in apostasy but in failure; not condemned but ineffective. Many of us are more Eli than we care to admit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eli's daughter-in-law, Phinehas's wife, goes into labor upon hearing the news. Dying in childbirth, she names her son Ichabod — 'the glory has departed' — and her last words are its repeated refrain.
verseByVerse.theology: Ichabod is simultaneously the epitaph of the Elide era and a question mark over all of Israel's future. The glory has departed — but the God of glory has not abandoned his people. He has simply refused to be tamed.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The ark's departure from Shiloh ended the central sanctuary era; Shiloh itself was eventually destroyed (Jer. 7:12). Now: The name Ichabod should be asked of any church or institution: is the glory still here? Not the program, not the tradition, not the building — but the manifest presence of the living God.

verseByVerse.quote: And she named the child Ichabod, saying, 'The glory has departed from Israel!' because the ark of God had been captured and because of her father-in-law and her husband. She said, 'The glory has departed from Israel, for the ark of God has been captured.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The name Ichabod — i-kabod, 'no glory' or 'where is the glory?' — is one of the most haunting proper nouns in all of Scripture. A woman dying in childbirth, whose husband has just been killed and whose father-in-law has just fallen dead, uses her last breath not to mourn her personal losses but to name the theological catastrophe: the glory has departed from Israel. She says it twice. The repetition is the narrator's way of letting the fact sink in. This is not merely military defeat; it is the departure of God's presence from among his people.

The glory — kabod — of the LORD was the visible, luminous presence of God that had been with Israel since the Exodus, that had filled the tabernacle (Ex. 40:34–35) and would later fill the temple (1 Kings 8:10–11). Its departure is not a metaphor; it is a theological event of the first order. Ezekiel will see it depart from Jerusalem in chapters 10–11 of his book, step by step, reluctantly. And in both cases, the same question hangs in the air: will the glory return? The answer, for those who have ears to hear, is Emmanuel — God with us — the one in whom the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14; the word is tabernacled), the one of whom it was said, we have seen his glory. Ichabod's question finds its final answer not in the ark's return to Israel but in the incarnation of the Son of God.

4.theology:
The God Who Cannot Be Tamed. The central theological lesson of chapter 4 is the utter impossibility of manipulating God through religious forms. Israel brought the ark and lost anyway. God cannot be deployed. He cannot be leveraged. He will not function as a cosmic lucky charm for a people who have not walked with him in obedience. Tim Keller calls this the 'vending machine view of God' — insert the right religious token, receive the desired outcome — and 1 Samuel 4 is its decisive refutation. God is not a force to be channeled; he is the Lord of hosts to be obeyed and trusted.

The Glory and the Question. Ichabod is not the end of the story but its most urgent question. The glory that departed from Shiloh would eventually return — to Solomon's temple, and then, after Ezekiel's vision of its departure, to the incarnate Son. Every time the church is tempted to rest in its forms, its buildings, its traditions, its reputation, the name Ichabod should ring: is the glory actually here? Not the echo of former glory but the present reality of the living God among his people.
4.examples:
Then: The loss of the ark to the Philistines was the end of Shiloh as a sanctuary — Psalm 78:60 and Jeremiah 7:12 both remember it as the moment God forsook his dwelling place. Israel had to learn that the place of God's presence is not fixed to a location or an object but to his own sovereign will.

Now: Churches decline when they confuse the forms of God's presence with the reality. Packed services, celebrated programs, historical reputation — none of these guarantee that God is actually at work. The answer to Ichabod is not better management but genuine repentance, renewed prayer, and faithful obedience to the word of God. Where these are present, the glory returns; where they are absent, no amount of religious activity compensates.

5.title: Dagon Falls Before the Ark
5.text: <sup>3</sup>And when the people of Ashdod rose early the next day, behold, Dagon had fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD. So they took Dagon and put him back in his place. <sup>4</sup>But when they rose early on the next morning, behold, Dagon had fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD, and the head of Dagon and both his hands were lying cut off on the threshold. (ESV)
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is one of the most darkly comic and theologically profound chapters in the Old Testament. Israel has brought the ark as a talisman and lost; the Philistines have captured it as a trophy. Now the ark begins its own sovereign campaign through Philistine territory, demonstrating that the God of Israel does not need Israel's army to fight his battles.

The chapter has a delicious irony at its heart. The Philistines place the ark in the house of Dagon — their chief deity, the fish-god — as if to say that Israel's God is now a vassal of Dagon. The next morning, Dagon is prostrate before the ark. They prop him up. The next morning, Dagon is prostrate again, and his head and hands have been cut off — the ancient gesture of complete defeat, done to kings and enemies. The god of the Philistines cannot stand in the presence of the God of Israel.

The theological message is clear: the ark's capture by the Philistines is not the defeat of God but the deployment of God. He has chosen to go into enemy territory not as a prisoner but as a conqueror. The plagues that strike the Philistine cities — tumors and panic — echo the plagues on Egypt. The God of the Exodus is the God of Ashdod and Gath and Ekron. He is Lord of the whole earth, not merely the patron deity of Israel.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistines place the ark in Dagon's temple as a trophy. Dagon falls twice: first prostrate, then dismembered. The threshold of Dagon's temple becomes untouchable — a monument to the judgment of the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: The idol falls before the true God; the false god cannot stand in the presence of the real one. This is the cosmic version of the first commandment enacted in history.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Placing a defeated enemy's god in your temple was standard ancient Near Eastern practice — it announced that your god had defeated theirs. The LORD reverses this narrative completely. Now: Every ideology, every competing loyalty, every idol eventually falls before Christ — either in surrender now or in final judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Philistines captured the ark of God, they brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod. Then the Philistines took the ark of God and brought it into the house of Dagon and set it up beside Dagon... And Dagon had fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD... the head of Dagon and both his hands were lying cut off on the threshold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Philistines have done exactly what ancient Near Eastern custom demanded: the defeated deity goes into the victor's temple. But the God of Israel is not a defeated deity — he is the living God, and within hours of his arrival, Dagon is on his face. The posture is significant: prostration before the ark is the posture of worship. Dagon, the chief god of the Philistines, is literally doing obeisance to the God of Israel. The Philistine priests find him the next morning and presumably think he has simply fallen over. They set him up. By the following morning, the message is unmistakable: Dagon's head and hands have been severed and lie on the threshold.

Head and hands: the head represents authority and identity; the hands represent power and action. Dagon has been rendered symbolically dead — he has no authority and no power. The threshold becomes a sacred boundary that Philistine priests will never cross again (v. 5). R. C. Sproul observes that this is a vivid enacted parable of Psalm 115:4–8: Their idols are silver and gold... they have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see... Those who make them become like them. The god who cannot stand before the LORD's ark is no god at all.

The arc of this narrative points forward to every confrontation between Christ and the powers. When the Word of God enters any domain — a heart, a culture, a temple — the false gods cannot stand. They are toppled not by human force but by the sheer presence of the living God. As Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 10:4–5: the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–12 — The Ark's Campaign Through Philistia
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD strikes Ashdod and its region with tumors and panic. The ark is moved to Gath, then to Ekron — and at each city, the same devastation follows. The Philistines cannot get rid of it fast enough.
verseByVerse.theology: The plagues echoing the Egyptian judgment make the theological point explicit: the God who delivered Israel from Egypt is the same God now active in Philistia. His sovereignty is not territorial.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Philistines' frantic city-to-city movement of the ark is a darkly comic portrait of people who have taken something they cannot handle. Now: The word of God and the presence of God are not comfortable possessions; they are either submitted to or fled from.

verseByVerse.quote: The hand of the LORD was heavy against the people of Ashdod, and he terrified and afflicted them with tumors, both Ashdod and its territory... So they sent and gathered all the lords of the Philistines and said, 'What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?' They answered, 'Let the ark of the God of Israel be brought around to Gath.'... But after they had brought it around, the hand of the LORD was against the city, causing a very great panic.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plagues on the Philistine cities are a deliberate echo of the plagues on Egypt. The hand of the LORD that was heavy on Pharaoh (Ex. 9:3) is heavy on Ashdod. The tumors (perhaps bubonic plague, or hemorrhoids) strike the whole region. Each city that receives the ark experiences the same devastation, and a desperate council of the Philistine lords debates what to do with this dangerous cargo they cannot manage.

The chapter's dark humor is unmistakable: the Philistines have captured the God of Israel — and discovered he is not capturable. They have a tiger by the tail. They cannot keep it and cannot safely release it. Their frustration is the frustration of everyone who has tried to handle the living God on human terms. The people of Ekron, receiving the ark, cry out: They have brought around to us the ark of the God of Israel to kill us and our people (v. 11). They are exactly right, though they do not understand why. The presence of the holy God is, as Hebrews 12:29 says, a consuming fire — not merely to enemies but to the unworthy handling of his glory. The ark's tour through Philistia is, in Sinclair Ferguson's phrase, 'the victory parade of the living God through enemy territory, attended by no army but carrying an irresistible power.'

5.theology: God Is His Own Defender. Israel could not defend the ark; they did not need to. The LORD of hosts defends his own glory with no assistance required. This is the message Chapters 5–6 together announce: God can work through Philistine territory, Philistine carts, and Philistine gold without a single Israelite soldier. The church's job is not to defend God but to trust him. When we act as if Christianity depends on our strategic brilliance, our political influence, our cultural credibility — we have forgotten the God who toppled Dagon and drove the Philistines mad with seven months of plague.
5.examples:
Then: The Philistines thought capturing the ark gave them a strategic advantage over Israel's God. They were catastrophically wrong. The lesson was learned at enormous cost across five cities.

Now: Every attempt to domesticate God — to keep him as a useful religious symbol while ignoring his actual demands — ends the same way. He will not be managed. He will not stay where he is put. And those who carry the name of Christ while refusing his lordship will find that his presence is not the source of blessing they expected.

6.title: The Ark Returns
6.text: <sup>12</sup>And the cows went straight in the direction of Beth-shemesh along one highway, lowing as they went. They turned neither to the right nor to the left, and the lords of the Philistines went after them as far as the border of Beth-shemesh. <sup>19</sup>And he struck some of the men of Beth-shemesh, because they looked upon the ark of the LORD. He struck seventy men of them. (ESV)
6.overview:
The ark's return to Israel is arranged by the Philistines with the help of their own priests and diviners, who understand enough about Israel's God to fear him. The elaborate test they devise — two nursing cows harnessed to a new cart, separated from their calves — is designed to determine whether the plagues were coincidence or divine judgment. The cows go straight to Beth-shemesh without deviation, mooing as they go, and the Philistine lords follow at a safe distance to watch.

The return of the ark is not an unqualified triumph. When the ark arrives at Beth-shemesh, some men look inside it and seventy of them die. The chapter ends not with joyful celebration but with frightened Israelites asking, Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? (v. 20). The ark's return does not resolve the spiritual crisis — it intensifies it. Israel has not yet grasped that the holiness of their God requires a corresponding holiness in those who approach him. The Philistines, pagans who had no covenant with God, have been punished with plagues; now Israelites, who had the covenant, are punished more severely for treating the ark with curiosity rather than reverence.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistine priests advise a guilt offering of gold tumors and gold mice, and a miraculous test: if the nursing cows leave their calves and go straight toward Israel, the plagues were from God.
verseByVerse.theology: The Philistine priests know more about Israel's God than many Israelites seem to. Their advice echoes the Exodus theology: do not harden your heart as Pharaoh did. Knowledge of God's power without covenantal relationship produces fear; knowledge with relationship should produce worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The gold guilt offerings — five tumors and five mice — acknowledge that the Philistine cities have sinned against the God of Israel, even without a formal covenant. Now: Even those outside the church recognize when they have been moving against the living God; the question is whether they will respond with genuine repentance or merely fear.

verseByVerse.quote: The Philistines called for the priests and the diviners and said, 'What shall we do with the ark of the LORD? Tell us with what we shall send it to its place.'
