They said, 'If you send away the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it empty, but by all means return him a guilt offering... Do not harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Philistine priests are among the most surprisingly perceptive figures in 1 Samuel. They know the story of the Exodus — why should you harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? (v. 6) — and they apply it correctly: resistance to the God of Israel is suicidal. Their advice is essentially: send the ark back with a generous guilt offering and test whether the disaster was providential or coincidental.

The guilt offering they prescribe — five gold tumors and five gold mice, one for each city afflicted — is a form of sympathetic acknowledgment of sin. They are not converting to Yahwism; they are making the prudent move of propitiation. And yet their advice contains a genuine insight: the God of Israel is not to be trifled with. Alistair Begg notes the irony that pagans here display more theological astuteness than many of God's own people: they recognize that the LORD's hand has been against them, they know the remedy involves acknowledgment of guilt, and they act. Meanwhile Israel in chapters 4–5 never repented at all.

verseByVerse.quote: The men did so, and took two milk cows and hitched them to the cart and shut up their calves at home. And they put the ark of the LORD on the cart and the box with the gold mice and the images of their tumors. And the cows went straight in the direction of Beth-shemesh along one highway, lowing as they went. They turned neither to the right nor to the left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two nursing cows walking away from their penned calves without deviation — lowing as they go, mourning the separation but obeying an unseen divine directive — is one of the most quietly miraculous scenes in the OT. Everything in their nature should have made them turn back. Nursing cows separated from their calves will always return to them; animal instinct is powerful and consistent. The only explanation for their straight path is divine compulsion.

The Philistine lords follow at a distance and watch, and they see what they needed to see: the disaster was not coincidence. It was the hand of Israel's God. They turn back at the border of Beth-shemesh, satisfied but still frightened. R. C. Sproul observes that this moment is a quiet but unmistakable public vindication of the LORD's honor: in full view of pagan lords, with no Israelite army present, the God of Israel directs nursing cows to bring his ark home. He needed no help. He never does.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Seventy men of Beth-shemesh look into the ark and die. The whole city mourns and asks who can stand before this holy God. They send word to Kiriath-jearim to come take the ark.
verseByVerse.theology: The death of the Beth-shemesh men is not arbitrary cruelty — the law explicitly forbade looking into the ark (Num. 4:20). Their curiosity violated the holiness of God. The same God who judged the Philistines also judges his own people, and at a higher standard.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Numbers 4:20 had been clear: the Kohathites could not even look at the holy things, lest they die. The Beth-shemesh men treat the ark's return as a tourist attraction. Now: Familiarity with sacred things — the Bible, the sacraments, corporate worship — can become a form of contempt. The holy God is not to be handled casually by those who think their long exposure has immunized them.

verseByVerse.quote: And he struck some of the men of Beth-shemesh, because they looked upon the ark of the LORD. He struck seventy men of them, and the people mourned because the LORD had struck the people with a great blow. Then the men of Beth-shemesh said, 'Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? And to whom shall he go up away from us?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The deaths at Beth-shemesh are shocking, and they are meant to be. The men who looked into the ark were Israelites — covenant people — and precisely because they were covenant people, the standard of reverence was higher. The Philistines received plagues; the Israelites receive death. Numbers 4:20 had been unambiguous: no one, not even the Levites designated to carry the ark, was permitted to look at the holy things. The Beth-shemesh men, curious and careless, looked — and died for it.

Their response is the correct one: Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? This is Israel's great theological question, and it will echo through the rest of the OT. Isaiah asks it in 6:5; the Psalms ask it repeatedly (Ps. 24:3; 130:3). The answer in the OT is: no one, apart from the mercy and provision of God. The answer in the NT is: the one Man who was perfectly holy stood in our place, bore our judgment, and now we can approach the throne of grace with confidence (Heb. 4:16) — not because we are holy but because he is, and we are in him. The question of Beth-shemesh is answered at the cross.

6.theology: The Holiness of God and the Problem of Approach. Chapters 4–6 together build the case that the holiness of God is the primary problem in Israel's life and in human life generally. The ark cannot be tamed by Israel (ch. 4), cannot be appropriated by the Philistines (ch. 5), and cannot be casually approached even by God's own people (ch. 6). The question at the end of chapter 6 — Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? — is the theological question that the whole sacrificial system was designed to answer, and that Jesus Christ answers perfectly and finally. He is the one who stood before God in our place and who now invites us to stand before God in his.
6.examples:
Then: The ark's journey from Aphek to Ashdod to Gath to Ekron to Beth-shemesh to Kiriath-jearim covers roughly forty miles and seven months (v. 1), leaving a trail of divine judgment. It arrives home not in triumph but in solemn, frightened recognition of the holy God.

Now: The chapter challenges two errors that persist in the contemporary church: the casualness that treats God's presence as no big deal, and the fear that treats it as unapproachable. Both errors misunderstand the gospel. The God who killed seventy at Beth-shemesh is the same God who gave his Son so that all who come through that Son find mercy, not judgment. Holy and gracious: never one without the other.

7.title: Return to the LORD
7.text: <sup>3</sup>'If you are returning to the LORD with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from among you and direct your heart to the LORD and serve him only, and he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines.' <sup>12</sup>Then Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen and called its name Ebenezer; for he said, 'Till now the LORD has helped us.' (ESV)
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is the pivot of the first major section of 1 Samuel. The ark has been in Kiriath-jearim for twenty years (v. 2), and a growing national lament has begun to stir — the people are yearning for the LORD. Samuel seizes the moment with pastoral directness: genuine return to the LORD requires putting away the foreign gods. No fence-sitting, no syncretism, no hedging bets. Put them away. Direct your heart to the LORD. Serve him only. When Israel obeys, the LORD himself defeats the Philistines at Mizpah — with thunder rather than with swords — and Samuel marks the victory with a stone named Ebenezer: Till now the LORD has helped us.

The chapter provides the blueprint for true revival: corporate lament (v. 2), prophetic challenge (v. 3), genuine repentance (v. 4), public fasting and confession (vv. 5–6), intercessory prayer (v. 9), and divine deliverance (vv. 10–11). Samuel is here fulfilling his triple role — prophet (calling the people to repentance), priest (interceding and offering sacrifice), and judge (leading the victory). He is the last great judge of Israel and the prototype of the triple office that will find its perfect expression in Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ark rests at Kiriath-jearim for twenty years while all Israel laments and seeks the LORD. Samuel's call to genuine repentance requires the complete removal of idols — no compromise with Baal or Ashtaroth.
verseByVerse.theology: True repentance is not merely turning toward God but turning away from idols. The two movements are inseparable: you cannot direct your heart to the LORD while keeping the Ashtaroth in the house. This is the logic of exclusive covenant love.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Baal and Ashtaroth represented fertility, prosperity, and military success — the Canaanite answer to all of life's fundamental needs. Israel kept them as insurance policies. Now: The contemporary equivalents — money, status, sexual freedom, self-determination — are kept for the same reason: we want God and our idols, just in case.

verseByVerse.quote: And those of the house of Israel lamented after the LORD. And Samuel said to all the house of Israel, 'If you are returning to the LORD with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from among you and direct your heart to the LORD and serve him only, and he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twenty years of the ark in Kiriath-jearim, twenty years of Philistine oppression, and something has finally broken. Israel lamented after the LORD — the Hebrew wayyinhau suggests mourning, sighing, aching for something lost. This is not mere political frustration at Philistine dominance; it is spiritual grief at the distance from God. Something in the national soul has been awakened, perhaps by the very severity of what God has done and permitted.

Samuel's response is a model of prophetic pastoral ministry. He does not simply offer comfort; he offers a condition. If you are returning to the LORD with all your heart — the 'if' is not a doubt but a demand. Genuine return requires radical action: put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth. The two must go together: the positive (direct your heart to the LORD) and the negative (put away the idols). Tim Keller writes that idolatry is not merely a sin among sins; it is the structural sin that organizes all other sins around it. Until Israel dismantles its idols, it cannot genuinely return to God, even if it continues to perform religious rituals. The same is true for every generation: repentance that does not include the actual removal of what competes with God's lordship is incomplete.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel assembles Israel at Mizpah for fasting and confession. When the Philistines attack, he offers a whole burnt offering and the LORD thunders against them, throwing them into panic. Israel pursues and defeats them.
verseByVerse.theology: The victory at Mizpah is entirely divine: the LORD thundered against the Philistines, not Israel's swords. This echoes the plagues in Egypt and anticipates the eschatological judgment of enemies. The people need only to pursue what God has already routed.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The burnt offering Samuel makes (a whole lamb) is his priestly act of intercession — he is acting for Israel before God. Now: Christ's sacrifice on behalf of his people is the antitype of every OT burnt offering, the one perfect intercession that secures what no human priest could guarantee.

verseByVerse.quote: Samuel said, 'Gather all Israel at Mizpah, and I will pray to the LORD for you.'... And Samuel took a nursing lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the LORD. And Samuel cried to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answered him. As Samuel was offering up the burnt offering, the Philistines drew near to attack Israel. But the LORD thundered with a mighty sound that day against the Philistines and threw them into confusion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The assembly at Mizpah is a remarkable act of corporate spirituality. Israel draws water and pours it out before the LORD — a gesture of total self-emptying, of pouring out the soul before God — and confesses: We have sinned against the LORD. Simple, unadorned, direct. No excuses, no qualifications, no blame-shifting. This is the kind of corporate confession that precedes genuine revival in every era of church history.

When the Philistines advance, it is Samuel's response that is telling: he does not organize the army, he does not give a battle speech, he offers a burnt offering and cries to the LORD. And the LORD answers with thunder. The divine warrior fights for Israel while Samuel intercedes — the same pattern as Moses on the hill with his arms raised while Joshua fought below (Ex. 17). The priestly intercession and the military victory are inseparable. Sinclair Ferguson observes that the victory at Mizpah is a microcosm of the entire Christian life: the battle is the LORD's, our calling is to prayer and repentance, and the outcome is his to provide. We pursue; he routs.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — Ebenezer: The Stone of Help
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel erects a memorial stone named Ebenezer — 'till now the LORD has helped us' — and summarizes his tenure as judge: the Philistines are subdued, peace is restored, Samuel circuits the land each year as judge.
verseByVerse.theology: The name Ebenezer looks back (the LORD has helped us) and forward (he will continue to help). It is a monument to divine faithfulness that calls future generations to trust the same God. Every act of remembering God's past faithfulness is an act of faith in his future faithfulness.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The stone at Mizpah marked the exact place where the LORD's thunderous deliverance occurred — a permanent sign that could be pointed to and explained to children. Now: The Christian has its own Ebenezers — conversion, answered prayer, preserved faith through trial — that the memory should cultivate and celebrate.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen and called its name Ebenezer; for he said, 'Till now the LORD has helped us.' So the Philistines were subdued and did not again enter the territory of Israel. And the hand of the LORD was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ebenezer — stone of help, or stone of the Helper. The name carries the entire theology of chapter 7 in three syllables. Not 'we fought and won,' but 'the LORD has helped us.' The victory belongs entirely to divine grace; Samuel marks it with a stone that will outlast both him and his generation, so that those who come after will ask, 'What is this stone?' and be told the story of God's deliverance. Memorialization is a spiritual discipline: the people of God are commanded to remember, to build altars and erect stones and tell the stories, precisely because memory of God's past faithfulness is the seedbed of present trust.

The summary of Samuel's judgeship in verses 15–17 describes a man whose entire life was organized around the service of God's people. He circulates annually — Bethel, Gilgal, Mizpah, and back to Ramah — bringing justice and maintaining the worship of the LORD. He is the last judge, and in him the judges era reaches its finest expression, even as it reaches its end. The same chapter that shows Samuel at his best will, in chapter 8, show the people asking for something different — something less dependent on God, more like the nations around them. The request for a king will undo what Ebenezer celebrated.

7.theology: The Pattern of True Revival. Chapter 7 is the OT's clearest pattern of genuine corporate renewal: lament (v. 2), prophetic challenge (v. 3), obedient repentance (v. 4), public confession (v. 6), intercessory prayer (v. 9), and divine deliverance (vv. 10–11). Every genuine revival in church history follows some version of this sequence. The initiative is God's; the response is human; the outcome is God's again. Jonathan Edwards, reflecting on the Great Awakening, described true revival as God pouring out his Spirit on a people who have been brought to the end of themselves — which is precisely the state of Israel after twenty years without the ark.
7.examples:
Then: Samuel's challenge to Israel in verse 3 was radical: complete renunciation of the Canaanite fertility gods. These were not abstract theological competitors; they were embedded in the social, agricultural, and economic life of Canaan. Giving them up was costly.

Now: The contemporary church faces the same call. The idols we maintain alongside our Christianity — the money we trust more than God, the approval we need more than his, the comfort we will not sacrifice — are the Baals and Ashtaroth of our generation. True return to the LORD requires their removal, not their management. And the promise attached is the same: serve him only, and he will deliver you.

8.title: Give Us a King
8.text: <sup>5</sup>'Behold, you are old and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations.' <sup>7</sup>And the LORD said to Samuel, 'Obey the voice of the people in all that they say to you, for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them.' (ESV)
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is the hinge of the entire book and one of the most theologically loaded chapters in the OT. The elders of Israel approach Samuel with a request that is, on its surface, entirely reasonable: Samuel is old, his sons are corrupt, and Israel needs strong, stable leadership. But God's response to Samuel reveals the theological depth of what has happened: they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them. The request for a king is not merely a political preference; it is an act of religious apostasy, a rejection of the divine kingship.

The chapter is a masterpiece of theological irony. God grants the request — with devastating clarity about what it will cost. Samuel's warning about the king's demands (vv. 11–18) is not political commentary; it is prophetic description. The king will take your sons for his army, your daughters for his household, your best fields and vineyards and oliveyards, a tenth of your grain and flocks. You will be his servants. And then: you will cry out because of your king, whom you have chosen for yourselves, but the LORD will not answer you in that day (v. 18). The warning is rejected: No! But there shall be a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations (vv. 19–20). Like all the nations — the phrase that reveals the spiritual diagnosis. Israel was never supposed to be like all the nations. Israel was supposed to be the LORD's peculiar treasure, his royal priesthood, his holy nation (Ex. 19:5–6). The desire to be 'like all the nations' is the desire to un-be Israel, to exchange the peculiar dignity of divine election for the ordinary mediocrity of human kingship.

Yet God's gracious sovereignty does not end here. He will give them a king — and through that king's failure, he will prepare the way for the true King, the Son of David, the one in whom divine and human kingship finally unite in the person of Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Request and Its Meaning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel's sons Joel and Abijah are corrupt judges at Beersheba. The elders of Israel demand a king like the nations. God tells Samuel: they have not rejected you but me.
verseByVerse.theology: The request for a king is theologically equivalent to idolatry: exchanging the LORD as king for a human substitute. The parallel in v. 8 — as they have forsaken me and served other gods, so they are doing to you — makes the connection explicit.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel's request is not unprecedented; God had anticipated it in Deut. 17:14–20. But the manner and motivation — 'like all the nations' — makes it sin rather than faithful planning. Now: Every generation of God's people is tempted to exchange his sufficiency for the world's solutions; the form changes, the theology remains.

verseByVerse.quote: When Samuel became old, he made his sons judges over Israel... Yet his sons did not walk in his ways but turned aside after gain. They took bribes and perverted justice. Then all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah and said to him, 'Behold, you are old and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samuel's sons are Joel and Abijah — their names mean 'Yahweh is God' and 'my father is Yahweh.' The irony is bitter. Sons with names that proclaim the covenant God turned aside after gain and perverted justice — the exact same sins as Eli's sons, the exact same pattern of priestly and judicial corruption that Samuel was raised up to replace. Samuel has not learned from Eli's failure; he has repeated it. The honored judge who kept Israel faithful could not keep his own household.

The elders' grievance is legitimate: Samuel's sons are corrupt. But their solution reveals a deeper problem. They ask not for better judges or a reformed system but for a king like all the nations. The phrase is the tell. Israel's entire history has been the story of a nation unlike all the nations — a people with the living God as their ruler, his law as their constitution, his tabernacle as their capital. The desire to be like all the nations is the desire to abandon this peculiar identity. R. C. Sproul writes that this request is Israel asking to give up its greatest privilege — the immediate kingship of God — in exchange for the comfortable normalcy of human government. It is the same trade every generation is tempted to make: exchange the demanding, glorious sovereignty of God for the predictable mediocrity of human alternatives.

verseByVerse.quote: But the thing displeased Samuel when they said, 'Give us a king to judge us.' And Samuel prayed to the LORD. And the LORD said to Samuel, 'Obey the voice of the people in all that they say to you, for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samuel's instinct is right: the thing displeases him. And his response is exactly right: he prays. He does not argue, does not acquiesce, does not rage — he brings it to God. And God's response to Samuel is one of the most extraordinary moments of divine self-disclosure in the entire OT. They have not rejected you — God sees Samuel's wound and addresses it first; the aging judge who has served faithfully all his life is not being personally repudiated. But then comes the theological weight: they have rejected me from being king over them.

God then draws the explicit parallel to the entire history of Israel: According to all the deeds that they have done, from the day I brought them up out of Egypt even to this day, forsaking me and serving other gods, so they are also doing to you. The request for a king is classified alongside idolatry. Not because human kingship is intrinsically sinful — God had anticipated it in Deuteronomy 17 — but because the motivation here is the rejection of divine rule. Calvin notes that the sin is not in the form of the request but in its content: they want a king instead of God, not under God. This distinction between theocratic kingship (David at his best) and autonomous kingship (Saul's self-reliance) will run through the rest of the book.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel delivers God's warning about the king's demands: military conscription, forced labor, taxation, and servitude. Israel refuses to listen. God tells Samuel to give them what they want.
verseByVerse.theology: The warning is God's final pastoral appeal before consent. Its repeated verb is 'take' — the king will take your sons, your daughters, your fields, your servants. The contrast with God's character (who gives, not takes) is unmistakable.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Samuel's warning proved exactly accurate. Solomon's taxation and forced labor eventually split the kingdom (1 Kings 12). The prophesied consequences arrived with full force. Now: Every human institution elevated above its proper role becomes a taker: demanding from its subjects what only God can rightly demand.

verseByVerse.quote: So Samuel told all the words of the LORD to the people who were asking for a king from him. He said, 'These will be the ways of the king who will reign over you: he will take your sons and appoint them to his chariots and to be his horsemen... He will take the best of your fields and vineyards and olive orchards and give them to his servants... you will cry out because of your king, whom you have chosen for yourselves, but the LORD will not answer you in that day.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word take appears six times in Samuel's warning. This is the grammar of human kingship at its worst: extraction rather than provision, conscription rather than calling, taxation rather than stewardship. Samuel is not describing an imaginary tyrant; he is describing the actual trajectory of every unchecked human power. Solomon will do precisely this (1 Kings 4–5; 9:15–21), and the rebellion of the northern tribes under Rehoboam will explicitly cite this oppression (1 Kings 12:4).

The final line of the warning is chilling: you will cry out because of your king, whom you have chosen for yourselves, but the LORD will not answer you in that day. The same God who answered Hannah's tears and Samuel's prayers and Israel's lament in chapter 7 will not answer the cry that comes from the consequences of deliberate choice against him. This is not God's abandonment; it is God's respect for human agency. They have chosen. They will experience their choice. Tim Keller writes that this is the terrifying logic of Romans 1:24–28 — God gives people over to what they insist on having, and the having is itself the judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: But the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel. And they said, 'No! But there shall be a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations, and that our king may judge us and go out before us and fight our battles.' And the LORD said to Samuel, 'Obey their voice and make them a king.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The finality of Israel's refusal is stark: No! — the single word in Hebrew — followed by we also may be like all the nations. After Samuel's solemn warning, after God's own diagnosis, after all of chapter 7's revival, this is their answer. They are not persuaded. They want a king who will fight their battles. The deep irony is that God has been fighting their battles all along — at the Red Sea, at Jericho, at Mizpah — but they want a visible human champion in armor, not an invisible divine warrior in thunder.

God's response is a kind of judicial consent: obey their voice and make them a king. He does not override their choice; he grants it, with full knowledge of where it will lead. This is one of the most sobering moments in Scripture: God saying yes to a request that he knows will bring suffering. It is not fatalism — God's purposes will ultimately be served even through the failure of human kingship, because the whole sorry history of Israel's kings will make the world desperately ready for the King who comes to serve rather than to take, to give his life rather than to conscript lives, to be the shepherd rather than the tyrant. The request for a king that begins in rejection of God will, in the fullness of time, produce the conditions in which God himself becomes King in the flesh.

8.theology:
The Rejection of God's Kingship. Chapter 8 identifies the deepest problem in the human heart: the refusal of God's direct rule. The Israelites' desire for a king 'like all the nations' is the political expression of the primal sin — the desire for autonomy, self-governance, freedom from the particular demands of the covenant God. R. C. Sproul argues that every human political instinct, left unchecked by grace, tends toward this: we want a visible, manageable human king rather than the invisible, demanding divine King. The solution to this is not better political systems but the coming of the King who is himself the servant — Jesus, who fulfills the hope of David while utterly subverting the pattern of Saul.

God's Strange Sovereignty. The most theologically vertiginous element of the chapter is God's consent: make them a king. He is not defeated by their refusal; he is working through it. The monarchy that begins in Israel's sin will produce David, and from David will come the Son of David, and through the Son of David the whole world will be blessed. God writes straight with crooked lines — but let no one conclude from this that the crookedness doesn't matter. The consequences of Israel's choice are real and costly. God redeems them; he does not pretend they weren't made.
8.examples:
Then: Israel had every reason to trust the divine kingship — the Exodus, the conquest, the judges, Mizpah — and they chose human kingship anyway. Their desire to be like the nations was not political pragmatism but spiritual retreat. The comfort of the visible overcame the discipline of the invisible.

Now: Every generation of God's people makes this same exchange in different forms. We want institutional solutions to spiritual problems; we want visible leaders to tell us what to think; we want the church to be impressive on the world's terms rather than faithful on God's terms. The answer to every version of this temptation is the same as it was in Samuel's day: direct your heart to the LORD and serve him only. He is not the king who takes — he is the King who gives, who gave himself, who gives life to all who come to him.

9.title: Saul the Seeker
9.text: <sup>2</sup>And he had a son whose name was Saul, a handsome young man. There was not a man among the people of Israel more handsome than he. From his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people. <sup>17</sup>When Samuel saw Saul, the LORD told him, 'Here is the man of whom I spoke to you! He it is who shall restrain my people.' (ESV)
9.overview:
Chapter 9 introduces Saul with deliberate irony. He is physically magnificent — tall, handsome, head and shoulders above everyone else — which is exactly what Israel asked for when they demanded a king 'like all the nations.' God is giving them precisely what they wanted, in precisely the form they would recognize as kingly. And the reader, having heard God's warning in chapter 8, is meant to feel the weight of that irony from the first description.

The chapter operates on two levels simultaneously. On the human level, it is a story about a young man looking for his father's lost donkeys who stumbles into a prophetic encounter that will change his life and Israel's history. On the divine level, it is a story of sovereign orchestration: the man God has chosen is guided step by step — by lost donkeys, by a servant's suggestion, by girls drawing water, by Samuel's advance preparation — into the position God has appointed for him. Saul's story begins with divine sovereignty so comprehensive that even the lost donkeys are instruments of providence.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Saul Looking for Donkeys, Finding a Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Kish's son Saul, strikingly handsome and tall, searches three days for his father's lost donkeys with a servant. The servant suggests consulting the man of God in the nearby city — Samuel.
verseByVerse.theology: The lost donkeys are the comic hinge of the narrative — God uses the most ordinary, undignified circumstances to bring his appointed king to his appointed prophet. Providence operates at the level of animal husbandry.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Saul has no idea he is about to be anointed king; he is worried about donkeys and his father's concern. Now: God's greatest callings often arrive through the most undramatic doors — a conversation, a book, a detour — and the person called is often the most surprised.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a man of Benjamin whose name was Kish... a man of wealth. And he had a son whose name was Saul, a handsome young man. There was not a man among the people of Israel more handsome than he. From his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people. Now the donkeys of Kish, Saul's father, were lost.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator's portrait of Saul is deliberately shaped to match Israel's request. They wanted a king 'like all the nations'; here is a man who looks like a king by any nation's standards. Tall, handsome, head and shoulders above the crowd — the physical description is almost a checklist of royal qualifications in the ancient world. Samuel will later be tempted to choose men on exactly these grounds (16:6–7), and God will correct him: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart. The contrast between Saul's physical impressiveness and spiritual inadequacy is established before he speaks a word.

The lost donkeys are a divine comedy at the level of everyday life. Kish's animals have wandered; Saul sets out to find them. Three days of searching through Ephraim, Shalishah, and Shaalim produce nothing. The servant suggests the man of God. One of the great themes of the chapter is the sovereignty of God working through the smallest contingencies: there would have been no kingship conference if the donkeys hadn't wandered, no meeting with Samuel if the servant hadn't suggested it, no meeting that day if the girls hadn't directed them to Samuel just before he left. Calvin delights in this kind of detailed providence — not a general oversight but a moment-by-moment superintending of human affairs toward divine ends.

verseByVerse.quote: As they were going into the city, they met young women coming out to draw water and said to them, 'Is the seer here?' They answered, 'He is; behold, he is just ahead of you. Hurry. He has come just now to the city, for the people have a sacrifice today on the high place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The timing is almost too perfect: Saul and his servant arrive in the city just as Samuel is about to go up to the high place for a sacrifice, just as the young women are coming to draw water, just as Samuel himself is coming toward them from the opposite direction. The convergence of timing — Saul arriving from three days of searching, Samuel having been told by God the day before to expect a man from Benjamin — is the fingerprint of divine providence working through ordinary human schedules.

The young women's answer is characteristically detailed and breathless: Hurry. He has come just now to the city, for the people have a sacrifice today. The urgency is not theirs but the story's — everything in this chapter is moving toward the encounter God has arranged. Alistair Begg observes that the chapter teaches us to look for God's hand in the interruptions and redirections of ordinary life: the detour that brought us somewhere we didn't plan to go, the conversation we stumbled into, the door that opened because another door closed. Saul's three days of fruitless donkey-searching prepared him, geographically and emotionally, for the moment of encounter with Samuel.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has already told Samuel: tomorrow I will send you a man from Benjamin — anoint him prince over my people. Samuel honors Saul at the feast and speaks privately with him on the roof, setting the stage for the anointing.
verseByVerse.theology: God's advance notification to Samuel — 'tomorrow, about this time' — shows that every element of this encounter has been divinely orchestrated. Samuel is not discovering God's will; he is executing it. The king Israel demanded is being given with sovereign precision.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Samuel treats Saul with honor — a place of prominence at the feast, the reserved choice portion, a private conversation. He is treating the future king as a king before anyone else sees it. Now: The ability to honor what God has appointed before it is publicly recognized is a mark of spiritual perception.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the day before Saul came, the LORD had revealed to Samuel: 'Tomorrow about this time I will send to you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you shall anoint him to be prince over my people Israel.' When Samuel saw Saul, the LORD told him, 'Here is the man of whom I spoke to you! He it is who shall restrain my people.' Then Saul approached Samuel in the gate and said, 'Tell me where is the house of the seer?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God's word to Samuel is beautifully precise: tomorrow about this time. Not 'someday a man will come from Benjamin' but 'tomorrow, approximately now.' The specificity of divine revelation is staggering and comforting simultaneously. God is not vague about his plans; he tells his servant exactly what to expect and when. And when Saul appears, the internal word of confirmation — Here is the man — requires no argument, no deliberation. The Spirit of God bears witness with Samuel's spirit.

Saul's response to learning that the donkeys have been found and that Israel's desire rests on him is a study in false humility — or perhaps genuine bewilderment: Am I not a Benjaminite, from the least of the tribes of Israel? And is not my clan the humblest of all the clans of the tribe of Benjamin? (v. 21). The words sound like the right words — and may be sincere here at the beginning. But the same Saul who protests his unworthiness in chapter 9 will later, in chapter 15, build a monument to himself and claim that he has performed the commandment of the LORD. The humility of the beginning and the arrogance of the end measure the tragedy of his story.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel took Saul and his young man and brought them into the hall and gave them a place at the head of those who had been invited... And Samuel said to the cook, 'Bring the portion I gave you, of which I said to you, Put it aside.' So the cook took up the leg and what was above it and set them before Saul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reserved portion — the thigh and the upper part — set aside specially for Saul is a royal honor. Samuel has prepared for this day; the feast has been organized in advance of Saul's arrival. The man who came looking for donkeys is being honored as a king before any public announcement. This private bestowal of honor, before the anointing, before the public proclamation, is consistent with how God typically works: the calling comes before the commissioning, the preparation before the announcement.

The private conversation on the roof (v. 25) — what was said is not recorded, which is itself significant — deepens the sense that Saul is being drawn into something whose full significance he does not yet understand. Samuel is building toward the anointing with pastoral care, allowing Saul time to absorb the reality of what is about to happen. The chapter ends with Samuel sending Saul's servant ahead so that he and Saul can stand still and hear the word of God — a model of the kind of attention the word of God deserves: clear the distractions, stand still, and listen.

9.theology: Providence in the Ordinary. Chapter 9 is one of the richest illustrations of divine providence in all of Scripture. God arranges lost donkeys, a servant's suggestion, girls drawing water, and Samuel's advance preparation into a sequence that brings his chosen king to his appointed prophet at exactly the right moment. R. C. Sproul notes that this kind of detailed providence — operating through the most mundane and seemingly chance occurrences — is the consistent testimony of Scripture: God is not sovereign over the dramatic moments only but over every contingency of every day.
9.examples:
Then: Saul begins his story as an apparently humble, obedient young man, doing his father's errands, honoring the prophet, bewildered by the honor being shown to him. The contrast with his later pride is part of the tragedy the book will trace.

Now: The chapter encourages the believer to trust God's providence in the apparent randomness of life. The detour that seems like failure may be the route God is using to bring you to the place he has prepared. The lost donkeys in your life — the setback, the detour, the failed plan — may be the very instruments of the greatest encounter of your life.

10.title: The Spirit of God Came Upon Him
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Samuel took a flask of oil and poured it on his head and kissed him and said, 'Has not the LORD anointed you to be prince over his people Israel? And you shall reign over the people of the LORD and you will save them from the hand of their surrounding enemies.' <sup>6</sup>'Then the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them and be turned into another man.' (ESV)
10.overview:
Chapter 10 records the private anointing of Saul by Samuel, confirmed by a series of three signs, and then the public selection by lot at Mizpah. The chapter is rich with the theology of election and the Spirit. The anointing is God's act through Samuel: the oil poured on Saul's head is not ceremonial decoration but the public marking of divine choice. And the promise that accompanies it — the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you — establishes that the empowerment for kingship is supernatural, not natural.

The three signs Samuel gives Saul are fulfilled exactly as predicted, and when Saul meets the band of prophets at Gibeah, the Spirit does rush upon him and he prophesies. The astonishment of those who know him — Is Saul also among the prophets? — captures the transformation in him. The Spirit's coming upon Saul here anticipates the Spirit's coming upon David at his anointing (16:13) and, ultimately, the Spirit descending on Jesus at his baptism (Luke 3:22). The anointing with oil and the coming of the Spirit are the double signature of divine appointment to royal office.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Private Anointing and Three Signs
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel anoints Saul with a flask of oil and gives three confirming signs: men at Rachel's tomb with bread, men at the oak of Tabor with goats and bread and wine, and prophets coming down from Gibeah with the Spirit rushing on Saul.
verseByVerse.theology: The three signs are not random — they are divinely calibrated confirmations that cover Saul's entire journey home, spacing the miracle of confirmation across time and geography. This is how God builds faith: step-by-step confirmation of what he has announced.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Anointing with oil in Israel was the formal act of consecrating priests and kings to their office — it was not merely symbolic but sacramental: an outward act accompanying an inner divine appointment. Now: The Spirit's work in the believer at conversion is the antitype — the anointing of which Saul's oil was a shadow (1 John 2:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel took a flask of oil and poured it on his head and kissed him and said, 'Has not the LORD anointed you to be prince over his people Israel?'... 'Then the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them and be turned into another man.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The anointing of Saul is one of the supreme acts of prophetic ministry in the OT. Samuel pours oil from a flask — not a horn (David's anointing in 16:13 uses a horn, a vessel of honor) but a flask, a more ordinary vessel — onto Saul's head and kisses him. The kiss is the mark of welcome and blessing; it accompanies the oil as a sign of personal affirmation alongside the official act. The question — Has not the LORD anointed you? — is rhetorical but fundamental: the anointing is God's act, Samuel merely the instrument.

The promise of the Spirit is the most important theological element of the anointing. The Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you — the word is the same used in Judges for the Spirit rushing on Samson and Gideon: an overwhelming, sudden, empowering presence. And the result: you will be turned into another man. This transformation is not moral (Saul's character will prove resilient to genuine sanctification) but functional: he will be equipped for the office to which he is called. The same pattern appears at Jesus' baptism, when the Spirit descends and the Father speaks: divine appointment confirmed by divine empowerment. Sinclair Ferguson writes that the Spirit who comes on the anointed one is the guarantee that the work of the king is God's work, not merely the king's.

verseByVerse.quote: When these signs meet you, do whatever your hand finds to do, for God is with you... And when they came to Gibeah, behold, a group of prophets met him, and the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied among them. And when all who knew him previously saw how he prophesied with the prophets, the people said to one another, 'What has come over the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fulfillment of the three signs is narrated with the same compressed precision as their announcement — each one happens exactly as Samuel said, in exactly the place predicted. When Saul meets the prophets at Gibeah and the Spirit rushes on him, the bystanders are bewildered: the tall farmer from Benjamin is prophesying with the prophetic guild. The proverb Is Saul also among the prophets? captures the surprise — he belongs to neither the professional prophets nor the priestly class, and yet the Spirit is upon him.

The transformation is genuine, even if temporary. The Saul who prophesies here is a different man from the Saul who will panic in chapter 13 and lie in chapter 15. The Spirit's empowering for office does not guarantee the permanent transformation of character — a sober warning that theological election and experiential sanctification are distinct. The Spirit can come upon a person for a specific task without producing the consistent fruit of the Spirit that marks genuine new birth. Saul's story is the tragedy of a man who receives the Spirit's power without the Spirit's persistent work of grace.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Mizpah, Israel is assembled and the king is selected by lot — tribe by tribe, clan by clan, man by man — until Saul is chosen. He is hiding among the baggage. The people shout 'Long live the king!' but some worthless fellows despise him.
verseByVerse.theology: The casting of lots in Israel was a means of discerning divine decision (Prov. 16:33). The lot falls on Saul not by chance but by God's sovereign direction. Yet even here the character study is revealing: the man chosen by God is hiding among the baggage.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The hiding among the baggage has been read two ways: genuine humility or paralyzing insecurity. The ambiguity is deliberate — it anticipates Saul's later pattern of fear and avoidance when God's demands become difficult. Now: The call of God does not automatically remove our instinct to hide when what is asked of us is costly and exposed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel near, and the tribe of Benjamin was taken by lot. He brought the tribe of Benjamin near by its clans, and the clan of the Matrites was taken by lot; and Saul the son of Kish was taken by lot. But when they sought him, he could not be found. So they inquired again of the LORD, 'Is there a man still to come?' and the LORD said, 'Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The public selection at Mizpah — the very place where Samuel had led Israel to repentance and victory in chapter 7 — is rich with irony. At Mizpah, Israel had poured out their hearts before God and received deliverance. Now they gather at Mizpah to formalize their rejection of God's kingship by installing a human one. The place of repentance becomes the place of royal accession.

The lots fall with mathematical precision: tribe, clan, family, man — narrowing to Saul. And Saul is hiding among the baggage. The interpretation has divided commentators. False humility, genuine terror, or the instinct of a man who already suspects he is not adequate for what is coming? The narrator does not resolve it. What is clear is that the man Israel is about to acclaim as king has to be found and brought out from behind the luggage. The contrast with David could not be sharper: David, when anointed privately by Samuel, is tending sheep — doing his work faithfully, not hiding from responsibility. The hiding is a first sign of the avoidance and denial that will eventually destroy Saul's kingdom.

The shout — Long live the king! — is Israel's first royal acclamation. And immediately afterward: some worthless fellows despise him (v. 27). The kingdom begins in division. Samuel, faithful to the end, writes out the rights of the kingdom in a book and lays it before the LORD — a provision for accountability that Saul will ignore.

10.theology: Anointing, Spirit, and Office. The double reality of oil and Spirit in Saul's commissioning establishes the theological grammar for all subsequent royal anointing in Israel. The oil is the outward sign; the Spirit is the inward reality. Without the Spirit, the oil is mere ritual; without the oil, the Spirit's coming has no public confirmation. This pattern reaches its apex in Jesus, whose very name — Christ, the Anointed One — encapsulates both: he is anointed by the Spirit at his baptism (Luke 3:22; Acts 10:38) and marked publicly as the royal Son. Every king before him is a shadow; he is the substance.
10.examples:
Then: The proverb 'Is Saul also among the prophets?' preserves in folk memory the remarkable moment of Saul's Spirit-empowered transformation. The bystanders could not explain it; they could only wonder at it.

Now: The chapter calls the church to distinguish between the gifts of the Spirit and the fruit of the Spirit. Saul had the gifts — the power, the transformation, the prophetic utterance — but not the abiding character that the Spirit produces in those who are truly renewed. The question for every person who has had a genuine spiritual experience is not 'did the Spirit come upon me?' but 'is the Spirit forming Christ in me?'

11.title: Saul's First Victory
11.text: <sup>6</sup>And the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled. <sup>13</sup>But Saul said, 'Not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel.' (ESV)
11.overview:
Chapter 11 shows Saul at his best: a man moved by the Spirit of God, rallying Israel to rescue the besieged city of Jabesh-gilead from the brutal Nahash the Ammonite, winning a decisive victory, and then extending mercy to his critics rather than revenge. It is a portrait of what Saul could have been — and it makes his eventual failure all the more tragic by showing us the genuine gifts he possessed.

Nahash's threat to gouge out the right eye of every inhabitant of Jabesh-gilead (v. 2) is one of the most grotesque opening gambits in the OT, and it is designed to provoke exactly the response it gets: terror and tears in Jabesh-gilead, outrage in Israel when the news arrives. When Saul hears, the Spirit of God rushes upon him — the same language as chapter 10 — and he mobilizes all Israel with dramatic speed. The victory is swift and complete, and Samuel wisely uses it to renew the kingdom at Gilgal with celebration and sacrifice.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead with the ultimatum of mass blinding. The Spirit of God rushes on Saul; he rallies three hundred thousand men and defeats Nahash by dawn.
verseByVerse.theology: The Spirit's role in Saul's military action continues the pattern of the judges: the Spirit enables what human capability cannot achieve. Saul here is acting as the last judge, not yet the self-reliant king he will become.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jabesh-gilead had a special connection to Benjamin from Judges 21; its rescue by Saul the Benjaminite resonates with tribal loyalty transformed into national solidarity. Now: The Spirit-empowered response to human suffering — not passivity but decisive, compassionate action — is a mark of genuine spiritual leadership.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Nahash the Ammonite went up and besieged Jabesh-gilead, and all the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, 'Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you.' But Nahash the Ammonite said to them, 'On this condition I will make a treaty with you, that I gouge out all your right eyes, and thus bring disgrace on all Israel.'... And the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nahash's ultimatum is not merely military cruelty; it is designed to humiliate. Gouging out the right eye would render every warrior in Jabesh-gilead unable to use a shield and fight effectively — the shield covers the left side, and the right eye looks over its rim. It is a calculated act of permanent degradation, designed to shame Israel before all its enemies. The response of the people is tears — helplessness before a power they cannot match.

Saul's response when the news reaches him is visceral and Spirit-driven. He is plowing in the field — doing the ordinary work of a farmer — when the messengers arrive with news that makes the people weep. The Spirit of God rushed upon Saul, and his anger is kindled. Not personal anger, not tribal pride, but righteous indignation at the humiliation of God's people. This is the best moment in Saul's story. He cuts up his oxen and sends the pieces throughout Israel as a call to arms — a dramatic, visceral summons that echoes the Levite in Judges 19–20. The response is overwhelming: three hundred thousand men from Israel and thirty thousand from Judah. The Spirit's work produces national unity around a crisis of justice.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul organizes Israel into three companies, attacks at dawn, and defeats Nahash decisively. He refuses to execute those who had despised him, attributing the victory to God. Samuel leads a renewal of the kingdom at Gilgal.
verseByVerse.theology: Saul's refusal to take revenge on his detractors is genuinely magnanimous and theologically grounded: 'Today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel.' When the victory belongs to God, personal vindication becomes irrelevant.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The celebration at Gilgal (the site of Israel's first camp in Canaan after the Jordan crossing) was a deliberate choice — renewing the kingdom at the place of original covenant entry. Now: The leader who uses victory to extend mercy rather than consolidate power images something of Christ, who uses his ultimate victory not to destroy enemies but to reconcile them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people said to Samuel, 'Who is it that said, Shall Saul reign over us? Bring the men, that we may put them to death.' But Saul said, 'Not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel.' Then Samuel said to the people, 'Come, let us go to Gilgal and there renew the kingdom.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The contrast between the people's vindictive impulse and Saul's gracious restraint is among the finest moments of his reign. The people, emboldened by victory, want to execute the doubters (the 'worthless fellows' of 10:27). Saul intervenes: Not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel. The theological ground of his mercy is exactly right: this is not his victory to exploit. It belongs to God.

This moment should be held in the mind when reading chapter 15, where Saul will keep Agag alive not from mercy but from pride, and disobey the explicit command of God. The same Saul who attributes victory to God in chapter 11 will take credit for obedience in chapter 15. The trajectory of his spiritual decline is precisely the increasing displacement of God from the center of his decision-making. What begins as Spirit-empowered God-centeredness ends in self-justifying disobedience. R. C. Sproul observes that spiritual decline in a leader rarely happens overnight — it is the slow, almost imperceptible replacement of 'the LORD has worked salvation' with 'I have performed the commandment.'

11.theology: Saul at His Best. Chapter 11 presents the ideal of Israelite kingship: a leader who is empowered by the Spirit, motivated by justice, capable of decisive action, and humble enough to deflect credit to God. The tragedy of 1 Samuel is not that Saul was always bad; it is that he could have been this and chose to become something else. The gifts were real; the failure was also real.
11.examples:
Then: The victory at Jabesh-gilead was long remembered — when Saul died, it was the men of Jabesh-gilead who walked all night to retrieve his body from the wall of Beth-shan (31:11–13), repaying the debt of their rescue.

Now: The chapter holds together the Spirit's enabling and the leader's responsibility. The Spirit's presence does not eliminate the need for courageous decision; it empowers it. But the Spirit-empowered leader must continually refer the victory back to God — the moment that stops, the empowerment begins to drain away.

12.title: Samuel's Farewell Charge
12.text: <sup>20</sup>'Do not be afraid; you have done all this evil. Yet do not turn aside from following the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart. <sup>22</sup>For the LORD will not forsake his people, for his great name's sake, because it is his good pleasure to make you his people.' (ESV)
12.overview:
Chapter 12 is Samuel's farewell address as judge, one of the great covenant speeches of the OT. It combines three movements: a vindication of Samuel's integrity (vv. 1–5), a rehearsal of God's covenant faithfulness through history (vv. 6–12), and a solemn charge to Israel for the future (vv. 13–25). At its center is one of the most tender verses in the book: the LORD will not forsake his people, for his great name's sake, because it is his good pleasure to make you his people (v. 22). Even in the context of Israel's sin in demanding a king, even after Samuel's solemn warning that further disobedience will destroy them, the bedrock promise of God's faithfulness holds.

Samuel confirms his integrity by inviting Israel to accuse him of any wrongdoing — and they cannot. He then leads them through salvation history as a pattern of warning: every time Israel abandoned God for other gods, they suffered; every time they cried to God, he delivered. The request for a king is the latest instance of this pattern. But Samuel does not end in condemnation; he ends in pastoral promise. He will keep praying for them. He will keep teaching them. And the LORD will not forsake his people. The door of repentance remains open.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — A Vindicated Prophet Rehearses History
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel challenges Israel to accuse him of any corruption — they cannot. He then recites salvation history: Exodus, judges, deliverance from enemies, all demonstrating God's faithfulness despite Israel's repeated apostasy.
verseByVerse.theology: The rehearsal of history is a covenant lawsuit form (cf. Micah 6): God presents his case through his prophet, demonstrating his faithfulness and Israel's unfaithfulness. The intent is not condemnation but repentance.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Samuel's personal integrity — 'whose ox have I taken? whose donkey have I taken?' — was the foundation of his prophetic authority. Now: The credibility of a messenger of God is inseparable from the character of his life; the word carried by a corrupt vessel loses its authority.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel said to all Israel, 'Behold, I have obeyed your voice in all that you have said to me and have made a king over you... Here I am; testify against me before the LORD and before his anointed. Whose ox have I taken? Or whose donkey have I taken? Or whom have I defrauded?... They said, 'You have not defrauded us or oppressed us or taken anything from any man's hand.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samuel's public self-examination is extraordinary in its boldness and confidence. He invites accusation. He names specific categories of abuse — oxen, donkeys, fraud, oppression, bribery — because these were the exact sins of his sons (8:3) and of Eli's sons before them. Samuel has lived in the light of the same scrutiny he now invites publicly. He has been the anti-Hophni, the anti-Abijah, and he knows it — not with pride but with the quiet confidence of a life examined before God.

Israel's response is unambiguous: You have not defrauded us or oppressed us or taken anything from any man's hand. This is the validation of an entire life of ministry. Forty years of circuit-riding, judging, praying, interceding — and not one person can bring a charge. John MacArthur notes that Samuel's farewell is the exact mirror image of the sons of Eli: where they took, he gave; where they corrupted, he served; where they abused power, he surrendered it. The credibility of Samuel's subsequent charge to Israel rests entirely on this foundation: he is a man who has no agenda except God's glory.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel said to the people, 'The LORD is witness... who brought your fathers up out of Egypt. If you will fear the LORD and serve him and obey his voice and not rebel against the commandment of the LORD, and if both you and the king who reigns over you will follow the LORD your God, it will be well. But if you will not obey the voice of the LORD, but rebel against the commandment of the LORD, then the hand of the LORD will be against you and your king.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samuel's rehearsal of salvation history follows the covenantal pattern of Deuteronomy: God's great acts of deliverance are recited as the ground of covenant obligation. The gift of the king is now placed within this framework: both king and people are under the same covenant obligation, the same promise of blessing for obedience and curse for disobedience. The monarchy does not change Israel's fundamental covenantal situation; it adds a new element of responsibility — the king must also obey.

The warning in verse 15 — the hand of the LORD will be against you and your king — is not vague threat but covenant promise operating in reverse. The same hand that delivered Israel at Mizpah will oppose Israel if they reject God's word. Calvin notes that Samuel's speech is a masterpiece of pastoral theology: it does not merely condemn the past but establishes the parameters for the future. The people can still choose well. The king can still obey. The door is not closed. The covenant is still operative. Judgment is not inevitable — but it is certain if the trajectory of apostasy continues.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–25 — The Sign of Thunder and the Great Promise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel calls down thunder and rain at wheat harvest — a miraculous sign — and the people fear greatly. Samuel promises to keep praying for them and not to sin by ceasing to intercede. The chapter ends with the great promise of God's faithfulness.
verseByVerse.theology: Samuel's declaration that ceasing to pray for Israel would be sin (v. 23) establishes intercessory prayer not as optional charity but as covenant obligation. The pastor who stops praying for his people has committed a sin against them and against God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Thunder and rain at wheat harvest (late spring/early summer) was climatically unprecedented in Canaan — a genuine miracle designed to authenticate Samuel's word and awaken Israel's fear of God. Now: The fear of God that authentic prophetic preaching produces is not psychological manipulation but the Spirit-wrought recognition of standing before the holy LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: Is it not wheat harvest today? I will call upon the LORD, that he may send thunder and rain... And the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel. And the people said to Samuel, 'Pray for your servants to the LORD your God, that we may not die.'... 'Moreover, as for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you, and I will instruct you in the good and the right way.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sign — thunder and rain in the wheat harvest — is both miracle and mercy. It is designed to awaken the people to the reality of what they have done (you have added to all your sins this evil, v. 19), and it works: the people are terrified and confess. Samuel's response to their fear is one of the most grace-saturated moments in the OT: Do not be afraid; you have done all this evil. Yet do not turn aside from following the LORD. The comfort is not that the sin doesn't matter — it does — but that the God who has been faithful through all of Israel's previous failures remains the God who does not forsake his people.

The pivotal verse is 22: the LORD will not forsake his people, for his great name's sake, because it is his good pleasure to make you his people. The ground of God's faithfulness is not Israel's performance but God's own character and purpose: his great name, his good pleasure. This is election theology at its most pastoral. Samuel does not say 'God will not forsake you because you have been faithful' — they haven't. He says 'God will not forsake you because of his own decision to make you his people.' This is the bedrock beneath every Israelite failure, and it is the bedrock beneath every Christian's assurance: God's faithfulness to his covenant depends on God, not on us. As Paul will put it: if we are faithless, he remains faithful — for he cannot deny himself (2 Tim. 2:13).

12.theology: The God Who Will Not Forsake. The great theological contribution of chapter 12 is the grounding of divine faithfulness in divine character rather than human performance. The LORD will not forsake his people for his great name's sake — his own honor is bound up in their preservation. This is the logic of the Psalms' appeal to God's name (Ps. 25:11; 79:9) and the logic of Paul's assurance in Romans 8:28–39: nothing can separate us from the love of God, because that love rests on his own eternal purpose and will, not on our fluctuating faithfulness.
12.examples:
Then: Samuel's farewell speech ended an era: the age of the judges was over, the age of the monarchy had begun. But the covenant framework in which both operated was unchanged. Kings come and go; the LORD's covenant with his people endures.

Now: The chapter is a pastoral model for every minister leaving a congregation: vindicate your integrity, rehearse God's faithfulness, charge them to obedience, promise to pray for them, and leave them with the bedrock of divine faithfulness. Samuel does not leave them with himself; he leaves them with God.

13.title: Saul's Presumptuous Sacrifice
13.text: <sup>13</sup>And Samuel said to Saul, 'You have done foolishly. You have not kept the command of the LORD your God, with which he commanded you. For then the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel forever. <sup>14</sup>But now your kingdom shall not continue. The LORD has sought out a man after his own heart, and the LORD has commanded him to be prince over his people, because you have not kept what the LORD commanded you.' (ESV)
13.overview:
Chapter 13 marks the beginning of Saul's end. The chapter has been waiting since the anointing: the test of obedience has come, and Saul fails it. The circumstances seem extenuating — the Philistines are gathering in vast numbers, his troops are scattering with fear, Samuel is seven days late arriving, and the situation demands action. Saul acts. He offers the burnt offering himself, in Samuel's place. And the moment he finishes, Samuel arrives.

Samuel's verdict is devastating in its precision: You have done foolishly. You have not kept the command of the LORD your God. The kingdom that could have continued forever over Saul's house will not continue. God has already identified the man who will replace him — a man after his own heart. The phrase anticipates David before David has appeared in the narrative, and it sets up the central contrast of the rest of the book: the king who acts from self-preservation versus the king who acts from love of God.

The military situation — Israelites hiding in caves and thickets while Philistine raiders devastate the land — frames the spiritual crisis. Saul's inability to wait for Samuel is not merely impatience; it is a failure of trust in God's timing and a grasping for the sacred prerogatives of another office. He plays priest when he is only king.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistines muster in overwhelming force; Saul's troops scatter in fear. With Samuel seven days late, Saul offers the burnt offering himself. Samuel arrives immediately and pronounces the kingdom forfeit.
verseByVerse.theology: Saul's sin is not primarily impatience but usurpation: he takes to himself the priestly office that belongs to another. The sin of Uzziah (2 Chron. 26:16–21) is the same: the king who reaches for the priest's role transgresses the God-ordained distinction between offices.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The seven-day wait Samuel had commanded (10:8) was a test of trust: would Saul trust God's timing even when the military situation seemed to demand immediate action? He would not. Now: The hardest form of obedience is often obedience in the crisis, when waiting seems irrational and acting seems necessary.

verseByVerse.quote: Saul waited seven days, the time appointed by Samuel. But Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the people were scattering from him. So Saul said, 'Bring the burnt offering here to me and the peace offerings.' And he offered the burnt offering. As soon as he had finished offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel came.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The timing is exquisite and merciless. Samuel does not arrive before the sacrifice — Saul completes it — and then Samuel walks in. The seven days had been commanded explicitly (10:8): Seven days you shall wait, until I come to you and show you what you shall do. Saul waited the full seven days. What he did not do was wait beyond them. The letter of the command allowed him one more hour, one more day — and he did not wait for it. He acted from fear of circumstance rather than trust in God's word.

The scattering of the troops is understandable: thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, troops like the sand of the seashore — the Philistine muster is overwhelming. Any military commander watching his force melt away would feel enormous pressure to act. R. C. Sproul writes that Saul's failure is the failure of faith in the crisis: he could not maintain trust in God's promise when the immediate situation seemed to contradict it. This is the test that faith is designed for — not the easy seasons when everything is going well, but the desperate moments when waiting seems to guarantee destruction.

verseByVerse.quote: Samuel said, 'What have you done?' And Saul said, 'When I saw that the people were scattering from me, and that you did not come within the days appointed, and that the Philistines had mustered at Michmash, I said, 'Now the Philistines will come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the LORD.' So I forced myself, and offered the burnt offering.' And Samuel said to Saul, 'You have done foolishly.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul's explanation is a masterpiece of self-justification. He enumerates the circumstances (the people were scattering, you did not come within the days, the Philistines had mustered), describes his emotional state (I said, I have not sought the favor of the LORD), and then delivers the most self-deceiving phrase in the passage: I forced myself. He presents his disobedience as reluctant necessity, an act of personal sacrifice for the greater good. He has turned sin into martyrdom.

Samuel's response ignores the explanation entirely and goes straight to the charge: You have done foolishly. You have not kept the command of the LORD your God. The circumstances were real. The pressure was genuine. The fear was understandable. None of it changes the verdict. Alistair Begg observes that the self-justifying mind is the most dangerous form of spiritual blindness: Saul genuinely believes he had no choice, which means he cannot repent, which means he cannot be forgiven. The tragedy of chapter 13 is not merely that Saul disobeyed but that he could not see it as disobedience. The sentence is stark: Your kingdom shall not continue. The LORD has sought out a man after his own heart.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistines control the metalworking trade, leaving Israel with only two swords in the entire army. Three raiding parties devastate the land while Saul and Jonathan sit at Gibeah with six hundred men.
verseByVerse.theology: The iron monopoly is both military fact and theological symbol: Israel has chosen a king to fight their battles, and now that king sits under a pomegranate tree with six hundred men while the enemy raids at will. Human kingship, chosen over divine rule, produces precisely the weakness Samuel warned about.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Philistine monopoly on ironworking was historically attested — controlling iron gave decisive military advantage in the early Iron Age. Now: The chapter is a picture of what it looks like when God withdraws his active blessing from a leader who has disobeyed: the external threats multiply while the resources diminish.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was no blacksmith to be found throughout all the land of Israel, for the Philistines said, 'Lest the Hebrews make themselves swords or spears.' But every one of the Israelites went down to the Philistines to sharpen his plowshare, his mattock, his axe, or his sickle... So on the day of the battle there was neither sword nor spear found in the hand of any of the people with Saul and Jonathan, except Saul and Jonathan themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The iron monopoly is one of the most vivid illustrations in all of Scripture of what political dependence looks like when it has no divine backing. Israel went to the Philistines to sharpen their agricultural tools — and paid for the privilege. They could farm but not fight. They had plowshares but not swords. The king they demanded to fight their battles has six hundred frightened men and two swords between them. The irony cuts to the heart of chapter 8: Israel wanted a king to fight their battles, and the king they got cannot arm his men.

But notice: Saul and Jonathan have swords. The chapter is setting up Jonathan's brilliant initiative in chapter 14 — the young man who trusts the LORD to act regardless of numbers or weapons — as the counterpoint to his father's faithless sacrifice. The contrast between Jonathan's faith and Saul's fear will run through chapters 13–14 like a thread of gold through a grey cloth, and it will deepen the portrait of David, who will eventually be the Jonathan-figure raised to the throne.

13.theology: The Man After God's Own Heart. The phrase a man after his own heart (v. 14) is one of the most important descriptions in all of Scripture. It does not mean a man who is sinless — David's story disproves that immediately. It means a man whose fundamental orientation is toward God, who, when he sins, comes back to God in genuine repentance rather than self-justification. The contrast with Saul is total: Saul's heart is oriented toward the opinions of the people and the preservation of his own position; David's heart, at its center, is oriented toward God. Both men will sin; the difference is in the direction of their returning.
13.examples:
Then: Saul's sacrifice at Gilgal was offered at the right place (the altar), at the right time (before battle), with the right materials — but without authorization, motivated by fear of men rather than fear of God. The form was correct; the heart was wrong.

Now: Every act of religious correctness motivated by fear of circumstances rather than love of God partakes of Saul's sin. The question is never 'did I follow the form?' but 'was the LORD the one I was serving?' True obedience waits for God's timing even when the circumstances demand immediacy.

14.title: Jonathan's Faith and Saul's Folly
14.text: <sup>6</sup>Jonathan said to the young man who carried his armor, 'Come, let us go over to the garrison of these uncircumcised. It may be that the LORD will work for us, for nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few.' <sup>45</sup>Then the people said to Saul, '... As the LORD lives, not one hair of his head shall fall to the ground, for he has worked with God today.' So the people ransomed Jonathan, so that he did not die. (ESV)
14.overview:
Chapter 14 is built around a profound and deliberate contrast: Jonathan's daring faith and Saul's compounding foolishness. Jonathan climbs a cliff with his armor-bearer to challenge a Philistine garrison of twenty men and triggers a rout that the LORD accompanies with earthquake and panic. Meanwhile, Saul makes a rash oath that will nearly cost him his son's life. The chapter shows the divergence between the spirit of faith and the spirit of fear operating in the same family, in the same battle, on the same day.

Jonathan's theology is concise and magnificent: It may be that the LORD will work for us, for nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few (v. 6). These twelve words are one of the great confessions of faith in the OT — a recognition that divine power is not constrained by numerical or military odds. They anticipate Gideon's three hundred, David and Goliath, and ultimately the cross: the LORD saves by few, by one, by the weak things of the world to shame the strong.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Without telling his father, Jonathan proposes a daring assault on the Philistine garrison. With his armor-bearer, he climbs to the pass and kills twenty men. The LORD sends a great panic through the Philistine camp.
verseByVerse.theology: Jonathan's action is not recklessness but faith-based initiative. He devises a sign to discern whether God is in it (vv. 9–10), and when the sign is given, he acts without hesitation. This is the model of the believer who tests the way, receives confirmation, and then moves decisively.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Philistine garrison outnumbered Jonathan by ten to one, and he was climbing on his hands and feet to reach them. The odds were laughable by human calculation. Now: Every act of gospel boldness — sharing faith, planting a church, confronting injustice — requires Jonathan's theology: 'Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few.'

verseByVerse.quote: Jonathan said to the young man who carried his armor, 'Come, let us go over to the garrison of these uncircumcised. It may be that the LORD will work for us, for nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few.' And his armor-bearer said to him, 'Do all that is in your heart. Do as you wish. Behold, I am with you heart and soul.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jonathan's opening speech to his armor-bearer is a compressed catechism of biblical faith. It may be — he does not presume on God but opens the door of possibility with reverent uncertainty. The LORD will work for us — the agency is entirely God's; Jonathan is not boasting in his own courage but in divine action. Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few — the mathematical reality of their situation (two against many) is simply irrelevant to someone who trusts an omnipotent God.

The armor-bearer's response is one of the great expressions of loyalty in Scripture: I am with you heart and soul. He does not ask for more information, more preparation, better odds. He commits wholly to the man he serves.
